title: Stochastic Simulation for Bayesian Modeling in Psychology
text:
Welcome
This website holds the released chapters of the book. You can also download it as a PDF.
Stochastic simulation provides a way to study Bayesian models when the quantities of interest are difficult to calculate directly. By generating draws from a probability distribution, we can estimate posterior means, probabilities, and predictions. This book develops the methods behind those calculations and shows how to implement them in R. Implementing the algorithms helps reveal how they work, why they sometimes perform poorly, and how to assess the results produced by statistical software.

title: Stochastic Simulation for Bayesian Modeling in Psychology
text:
Why we wrote this book
We previously taught two separate courses in the Research Master’s Psychology program at the University of Amsterdam. One used Bayes Rules! (Johnson et al., 2022), and the other used MCMC from Scratch (Hanada & Matsuura, 2022). Both are excellent books, but they differ in the topics they cover, the depth of their treatment, and the technical background they expect. Bayes Rules! introduces Bayesian modeling through applications, while MCMC from Scratch develops the principles and implementation of Monte Carlo methods.
Bringing the two courses together required a text that connected introductory Bayesian modeling with a more detailed study of simulation algorithms. We could not find a book that matched that combination of topics and level. We wrote this book to fill the gap, working through the explanations, mathematical steps, and code needed to understand and implement the methods.

title: Stochastic Simulation for Bayesian Modeling in Psychology
Stochastic Simulation for Bayesian Modeling in Psychology
text:
How this book is organized
The book has five parts. Each builds on the concepts and methods introduced earlier.
Foundations. 1  Probability and Simulation introduces Monte Carlo integration, explains its accuracy, and develops methods for generating random draws. 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited connects these ideas to Bayesian inference, including posterior summaries, marginal likelihoods, and Bayes factors. These chapters also explain why obtaining useful draws and evaluating integrals become more demanding as models grow.
Markov Chains. 3  Markov Chains develops the properties of Markov chains and explains how their transitions can be constructed to preserve a chosen stationary distribution. 4  Diagnosing Markov Chains uses simulations from Stan to introduce practical checks of chain behavior and estimates of Monte Carlo accuracy.
Sampling Algorithms. 5  The Metropolis Algorithm develops the Metropolis algorithm using ratios of posterior densities. 6  Adaptive Metropolis turns it into a procedure that tunes its own step size, by way of the Robbins–Monro procedure. 7  The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm generalizes the proposal distribution and introduces the independence sampler. Chapter 8 (Gibbs Sampling and Metropolis-within-Gibbs) introduces updates from conditional distributions and combines them with Metropolis steps when direct conditional sampling is unavailable. The code makes the connection between each algorithm’s mathematical definition and its implementation explicit.
Model Uncertainty. Chapter 9 (Bayesian Variable Selection) treats the inclusion of predictors as an unknown part of a regression model. Chapter 10 (Bayesian Model Averaging) uses posterior model probabilities to combine estimates and predictions across models, accounting for uncertainty about model choice.
Going Further. Chapter 11 (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) introduces Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, the family of methods underlying Stan’s sampling algorithms. This chapter is optional; the earlier chapters can be studied independently of it.

title: Stochastic Simulation for Bayesian Modeling in Psychology
text:
How to read this book
Each chapter introduces a problem and its learning goals, develops the methods through worked examples, and closes with a summary and exercises. Read the explanations alongside the code, run the examples, and examine how the results change when you alter the inputs or simulation settings.
The appendices provide software guidance, a reference for notation, and detailed mathematical derivations that supplement the main explanations.
The exercises take three forms. Conceptual exercises ask you to explain or derive an idea. Practical exercises develop your ability to implement and assess a method. Applied exercises use the methods to answer questions about data.


Definitions and algorithms

Gray boxes collect definitions, algorithms, and short summaries for reference while you work through the examples and exercises.



Quiz yourself!

Quiz boxes offer a question to consider before continuing. Try to formulate an answer, then compare it with the answers collected near the end of the chapter.

title: Stochastic Simulation for Bayesian Modeling in Psychology
text:
Software
The examples use R. The tidyverse supports data manipulation and plotting, rstan provides an interface to Stan, and bayesplot and posterior provide tools for examining simulation output. Appendix A — Software Setup gives installation instructions and help with common setup problems.

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.1 Random variables, densities, and expectations
Suppose you run a stop-signal task. A participant sees an arrow and presses a key as quickly as possible. On some trials, a tone sounds shortly after the arrow, telling the participant to withhold the response. One account of this task treats it as a race between a go process and a stop process (Logan & Cowan, 1984). The go process starts when the arrow appears; the stop process starts when the tone sounds. The participant stops successfully if the stop process finishes first.
If you specify distributions for the durations of these processes, how can you calculate the probability of stopping? One approach is to simulate many races and calculate the proportion in which the stop process wins. This proportion is a Monte Carlo estimate. It lets you study a model’s predictions even when calculating them directly is difficult.
This chapter develops that approach. We begin with probability distributions and expectations, use simulation to approximate them, and examine the accuracy of the resulting estimates. We then study how to generate draws from a distribution and why some sampling methods become inefficient. For further background on probability, simulation, and Bayesian inference, see Bayes Rules! (Johnson et al., 2022, Chapters 2, 3 and 8).
The code assumes that you can assign objects, call functions, and work with vectors in R. Run the following setup before working through the examples. Every chunk that generates random numbers starts with set.seed(84735), so you can run any chunk on its own and obtain the numbers printed in the book.
We use \(N\) for the number of Monte Carlo draws and \(n\) for the number of observed data points. The distinction matters because increasing \(N\) makes a computation more precise, whereas increasing \(n\) adds information about the phenomenon being studied.
A random variable \(X\) is a quantity whose value is uncertain, and a probability distribution says how that uncertainty is spread over the possible values. When \(X\) is discrete, a probability mass function \(f(x) = P(X = x)\) assigns a probability to each value. When \(X\) is continuous, a probability density function \(f(x)\) assigns a density to each value, and probabilities are areas under it: \(P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). In both cases \(f\) is non-negative and the total probability is one. We write densities and mass functions as \(f(\cdot)\), with the argument indicating the variable concerned. Uppercase \(X\) denotes a random variable; lowercase \(x\) denotes a possible value. For a continuous variable, the density at a point is not a probability. Probabilities come from areas over intervals, and a density can exceed one.
Our running example concerns Nederlandse Spoorwegen (NS), the Dutch national railway operator. Sara commutes between Amsterdam and Utrecht and wants to learn the probability \(\pi\) that a train on her route arrives on time. For this example, she defines “on time” as no more than three minutes late and treats the journeys as independent, with the same on-time probability.
Before collecting data, Sara represents her uncertainty about \(\pi\) with a prior distribution, \(\pi \sim \text{Beta}(7,5)\). The symbol \(\sim\) means “has distribution”. A Beta distribution is defined on \([0,1]\), making it useful for an unknown probability. Its two positive shape parameters determine its shape; its mean is \(a/(a+b)\) for a \(\text{Beta}(a,b)\) distribution. Sara’s illustrative prior therefore has mean \(7/12 \approx 0.58\). It describes uncertainty about the on-time probability, rather than the variation between individual trains.
prior_grid <- tibble(p = seq(0, 1, length.out = 501), density = dbeta(p, 7, 5))
ggplot(prior_grid, aes(p, density)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(prior_grid, p >= 0.8), fill = "#552E6B", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(color = "#552E6B") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 7/12, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "On-time probability", y = "Prior density")







Figure 1.1: Sara’s Beta(7,5) prior. The dashed line marks its mean, 7/12. The shaded area is the prior probability that the on-time rate exceeds 0.8; the height of the curve at 0.8 is not that probability.
In Figure 1.1, the whole area under the curve is one. The small shaded area expresses how little prior probability Sara assigns to on-time rates above 0.8.
The expectation of a function \(g\) of \(X\) is the average of \(g(X)\), weighted by how probable each value is, \[
E[g(X)] = \sum_{x} g(x)\, f(x) \quad \text{(discrete)}, \qquad
E[g(X)] = \int g(x)\, f(x)\,dx \quad \text{(continuous)}.
\] For discrete \(X\), the sum runs over its possible values. Each term multiplies \(g(x)\) by the probability mass \(f(x)=P(X=x)\). For continuous \(X\), we instead multiply \(g(x)\) by the probability density \(f(x)\) and integrate over the support of \(X\), the set of possible values. The density at \(x\) is not the probability of that individual value; probabilities are obtained by integrating the density over intervals. For example, if \(X\) indicates whether a train is on time and \(P(X=1)=0.8\), then \(E[X]=0\times 0.2+1\times 0.8=0.8\).
The function \(g\) specifies what we want to average. The mean is \(E[X]\), with \(g(x) = x\). The variance is \(E[(X - \mu)^2]\). For a variable \(X\) supported on \([0,1]\), a probability is an expectation too. If \(\mathbb{1}\{X > 0.8\}\) is the indicator that equals one when \(X > 0.8\) and zero otherwise, then \[
P(X > 0.8) = \int_{0.8}^{1} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^1 \mathbb{1}\{x > 0.8\}\, f(x)\,dx = E\!\left[\mathbb{1}\{X > 0.8\}\right].
\]
For Sara’s prior we can compute these integrals exactly, because the Beta family is well studied. The probability that the on-time rate exceeds 0.8 is a Beta integral, and R’s pbeta() knows the answer. We can also hand the integral to a numerical routine that knows nothing about the Beta family:
1 - pbeta(0.8, shape1 = 7, shape2 = 5)
#> [1] 0.05040957
integrate(function(p) dbeta(p, 7, 5), lower = 0.8, upper = 1)
#> 0.05040957 with absolute error < 5.6e-16
integrate(function(p) p * dbeta(p, 7, 5), lower = 0, upper = 1)
#> 0.5833333 with absolute error < 6.5e-15
The last line computes the prior mean, \(7/12 \approx 0.583\). The function dbeta() evaluates a Beta density, whereas pbeta() returns the area to the left of its first argument. Thus 1 - pbeta(0.8, 7, 5) gives the shaded area in Figure 1.1. In the second line, integrate() computes that same area numerically; its reported absolute error concerns numerical integration, not uncertainty about \(\pi\).
Numerical integration is often effective for one parameter. Extending a simple grid to many parameters can be costly. With 100 evaluation points for each of ten parameters, a full grid contains \(100^{10}=10^{20}\) combinations. R’s integrate() is an adaptive one-dimensional routine, rather than such a multidimensional grid. With many parameters, evaluating every combination of grid points quickly becomes impractical. Monte Carlo offers another approach: Draw combinations of parameter values from the distribution and use them to estimate the quantity of interest.

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
Expressing summaries as expectations

For discrete \(X\), use \(E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)f(x)\). For continuous \(X\), use \(E[g(X)]=\int g(x)f(x)\,dx\), integrating over its support. Choosing \(g(x)=x\) gives the mean; choosing \(g(x)=(x-\mu)^2\), where \(\mu=E[X]\), gives the variance. An indicator function gives an event probability. These expectations must exist for the corresponding summary to be defined.







Quiz yourself!

Sara wants the probability that the on-time rate is between 0.6 and 0.8. Write this probability as an expectation \(E[g(\pi)]\). What is \(g\)?

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.2 Pseudo-random numbers in R
Simulation needs random numbers, and lots of them. The generators we use produce pseudo-random numbers. These are deterministic sequences designed to behave like random draws for statistical computation. The classic recipe is the linear congruential generator, which starts from a seed \(x_0\) and repeats \[
x_{t+1} = (a\, x_t + b) \bmod M,
\] so that each number is an arithmetic function of the previous one (Hanada & Matsuura, 2022, Section 2.1). The operation “modulo \(M\)” returns the remainder after division by \(M\); R writes it as %%. For example, \((5\times7+3)\bmod16=6\). Here is a toy version with only 16 possible states. It illustrates repetition, but is not suitable for statistical work:

lcg <- function(N, seed, a = 5, b = 3, M = 16) {
  x <- numeric(N)
  x[1] <- seed
  if (N > 1) for (t in 2:N) x[t] <- (a * x[t - 1] + b) %% M
  x / M
}
lcg(20, seed = 7)
#>  [1] 0.4375 0.3750 0.0625 0.5000 0.6875 0.6250 0.3125 0.7500 0.9375 0.8750
#> [11] 0.5625 0.0000 0.1875 0.1250 0.8125 0.2500 0.4375 0.3750 0.0625 0.5000

The same seed gives the same sequence. With \(M=16\), there are only 16 possible states, so a state must eventually repeat. In this example the full sequence repeats after 16 values. Practical generators use much larger state spaces and more sophisticated recurrences. R’s default, the Mersenne Twister, has a period of \(2^{19937} - 1\), so the short repeating pattern of this toy example is avoided.
In R, runif(N) gives \(N\) pseudo-random numbers that are uniform on \((0, 1)\), and set.seed() fixes the seed, which is what makes a simulation reproducible:

set.seed(2026)
runif(3)
#> [1] 0.6986735 0.5565305 0.1401400
set.seed(2026)
runif(3)
#> [1] 0.6986735 0.5565305 0.1401400

A seed reproduces a calculation when the generator, software, and sequence of random-number calls are the same. Resetting the same seed on every iteration restarts the sequence, so repeated calls can produce identical draws. Set the seed before a simulation rather than inside its sampling loop.
For reproducible work, record sessionInfo() and RNGkind() along with the code and seed. Changes in R or package versions can change results, and platform-dependent numerical calculations can differ slightly. R’s RNGversion() can restore earlier generator settings when reproducing older code; a seed alone does not record the full computing environment see the R documentation.
Uniform draws can also be transformed into draws from other distributions. For example, a uniform draw is below 0.8 with probability 0.8, so as.integer(runif(1) < 0.8) simulates an on-time indicator. We develop this idea further in the section on inverse-transform sampling.
R uses a consistent naming system for distribution functions:








Prefix
Meaning
Beta example




d
Density, or probability mass for a discrete variable
dbeta(0.8, 7, 5)


p
Cumulative probability \(P(X\le x)\)
pbeta(0.8, 7, 5)


q
Quantile, the value at a specified cumulative probability
qbeta(0.95, 7, 5)


r
Random draws
rbeta(1000, 7, 5)



The same prefixes apply to norm, binom, exp, and many other families. A quantile answers the reverse of a cumulative-probability question. For instance, qbeta(0.95, 7, 5) is the value below which 95% of Sara’s prior probability lies.

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.3 Monte Carlo integration
We first estimate the mathematical constant \(\pi\approx3.14159\) using points drawn in a square (Hanada & Matsuura, 2022, Section 2.2). In this example only, \(\pi\) denotes the circle constant, not Sara’s on-time probability.
A circle of radius \(r\) has area \(\pi r^2\). A quarter of a circle of radius one therefore has area \(\pi/4\). Place it in the unit square, whose horizontal and vertical coordinates both range from zero to one. The square has area one. If points are drawn uniformly across the square, the probability of falling in the quarter circle equals its fraction of the square’s area, \((\pi/4)/1=\pi/4\).








Figure 1.2: The geometry before simulation. A point (x,y) is inside the shaded quarter circle when its distance from the origin is at most one. The example point (0.6,0.5) satisfies 0.6 squared + 0.5 squared = 0.61 < 1.





The distance from the origin to \((x,y)\) is \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) by Pythagoras’ theorem. Thus a point is inside when \(x^2+y^2\le1\) (Figure 1.2). To simulate a point, draw its horizontal coordinate with runif() and its vertical coordinate independently with another call. Entry i of x and entry i of y form point i.
The expression x^2 + y^2 <= 1 checks the condition for every point and returns TRUE or FALSE. When averaged, R treats these as one or zero. The resulting proportion estimates \(\pi/4\), so multiplying by four estimates \(\pi\).

set.seed(84735)
N <- 10000
x <- runif(N)
y <- runif(N)
inside <- x^2 + y^2 <= 1
4 * mean(inside)
#> [1] 3.1616


darts <- tibble(x, y, inside)
running <- tibble(n_darts = seq_len(N), estimate = 4 * cumsum(inside) / n_darts)

p_darts <- darts |>
  slice_head(n = 2000) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = inside)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#552E6B", "FALSE" = "#ECECEC"), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_running <- ggplot(running, aes(n_darts, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pi, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = "#552E6B") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of darts (log scale)", y = expression(hat(pi)))

wrap_plots(p_darts, p_running, widths = c(1, 1.6))







Figure 1.3: Estimating \(\pi\) by throwing darts. Left: the first 2,000 darts; those inside the quarter circle are purple. Right: four times the running proportion of darts inside, as the number of darts grows. The estimate wanders at first and settles down toward \(\pi\) (dashed line).





Why does this work? Write \(I_i\) for the indicator that dart \(i\) lands inside. Each \(I_i\) is a random variable with \(E[I_i] = P(\text{inside}) = \pi/4\), and the darts are independent. The Law of Large Numbers states that an average of independent, identically distributed draws converges to its expectation, provided the absolute expectation is finite. The condition holds here because the indicators are bounded between zero and one. So \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i I_i \to \pi/4\), and our estimate \(4 \bar{I} \to \pi\). The right panel of Figure 1.3 is the Law of Large Numbers in action.
Now look at what we did in the language of the previous section. The darts \((X, Y)\) are draws from the uniform density on the unit square, and \(\pi/4 = E[\mathbb{1}\{X^2 + Y^2 \le 1\}]\) is an expectation under that density. We estimated an integral by drawing from the density and averaging the function. The same averaging procedure applies to other distributions and functions.


Monte Carlo integration

To approximate \(E[g(X)]\), defined by a sum or integral:

Draw \(X^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(N)}\) independently from \(f\).
Compute the average \(\bar{g} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} g(X^{(i)})\).

When \(E[|g(X)|]<\infty\), the Law of Large Numbers implies that \(\bar{g} \to E[g(X)]\) as \(N \to \infty\). If \(g(X)\) also has finite variance, the Monte Carlo standard error of \(\bar{g}\) is \[
\text{SE}(\bar{g}) = \frac{\text{sd}(g(X))}{\sqrt{N}} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(g(X^{(i)}) - \bar{g}\right)^2},
\] and for large \(N\) the estimate is approximately Normal, so \(\bar{g} \pm 2\,\text{SE}\) is an approximate 95% confidence interval for the expectation being estimated. This uses the Central Limit Theorem and a finite, nonzero variance; it is not a guarantee for every simulation size.


1.3.1 How accurate is it?
The right panel of Figure 1.3 shows the estimate settling down, but with 10,000 darts it has not necessarily arrived; our run gives \(3.162\) against \(\pi \approx 3.1416\). How far off should we expect it to be? The estimate is an average of independent draws of \(g(X, Y) = 4 \cdot \mathbb{1}\{X^2 + Y^2 \le 1\}\), so the Central Limit Theorem applies: the average is approximately Normal with mean \(\pi\) and standard deviation \(\text{sd}(g)/\sqrt{N}\). We can estimate \(\text{sd}(g)\) from the same draws:

g <- 4 * inside
estimate <- mean(g)
mc_se <- sd(g) / sqrt(N)
c(estimate = estimate, se = mc_se)
#>   estimate         se 
#> 3.16160000 0.01628174

Our estimate of \(\pi\) is \(3.162\), with estimated standard error \(0.016\). Its approximate 95% Monte Carlo confidence interval is \[
[3.129,\; 3.194].
\] If we repeated the entire simulation many times and constructed a confidence interval from each simulation, approximately 95% of these intervals would contain the true value of \(\pi\). This interval describes uncertainty from using finitely many simulated points. It does not describe uncertainty about a participant or a railway parameter.
The standard error decreases at rate \(1/\sqrt{N}\). For example, increasing the number of darts from 10,000 to 40,000 halves the standard error; increasing it to 1,000,000 reduces it by a factor of ten. These statements concern the typical size of simulation error. An individual estimate need not move closer to the truth every time more draws are added.


Quiz yourself!

If you quadruple the number of darts, by what factor does the Monte Carlo standard error shrink? Using \(\text{SE}=\sqrt{\pi(4-\pi)/N}\), how many darts are needed for an approximate 95% confidence interval with half-width 0.001? You may use \(\pi\approx3.14159\) for this planning calculation.

Let’s check the \(1/\sqrt{N}\) rule directly by repeating the whole experiment 200 times for three sample sizes and looking at the spread of the estimates.

set.seed(84735)
estimate_pi <- function(N) 4 * mean(runif(N)^2 + runif(N)^2 <= 1)

repeats <- expand_grid(N = c(100, 1000, 10000), rep = 1:200) |>
  mutate(estimate = map_dbl(N, estimate_pi))

repeats |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(N), estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pi, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, seed = 1),
             alpha = 0.3, color = "#552E6B", size = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Number of darts", y = expression(hat(pi)))







Figure 1.4: Two hundred independent estimates of \(\pi\) for each of three numbers of darts. The spread shrinks by a factor of about \(\sqrt{10}\) each time the number of darts grows tenfold.






repeats |>
  group_by(N) |>
  summarize(observed_sd = sd(estimate)) |>
  mutate(theoretical_se = sqrt(pi * (4 - pi) / N))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>       N observed_sd theoretical_se
#>   <dbl>       <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1   100      0.163          0.164 
#> 2  1000      0.0527         0.0519
#> 3 10000      0.0158         0.0164

The observed standard deviation of the estimates matches the theoretical standard error \(\sqrt{\pi(4 - \pi)/N}\), which follows from the variance of the indicator, \(\text{Var}(4 I) = 16 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{4}(1 - \tfrac{\pi}{4}) = \pi(4 - \pi)\). Each row uses ten times as many darts as the one above it and is about \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) times more precise.


1.3.2 The recipe in general
The Monte Carlo recipe applies whenever we can generate independent draws from the required distribution and evaluate a function with a finite expectation. Return to the stop-signal task. For illustration, let the go duration be the sum of a Normal variable with mean 500 ms and standard deviation 50 ms and an Exponential variable with mean 100 ms. Such a sum is called an ex-Gaussian variable. Let the stop duration be a Normal variable with mean 200 ms and standard deviation 30 ms plus an Exponential variable with mean 50 ms. These choices illustrate the computation rather than estimates from a particular experiment.
We assume that the components and the two processes are independent. All finishing times must be measured from the same starting point. The go process begins at the arrow, whereas the stop process begins 250 ms later. We therefore add 250 to the simulated stop duration before comparing the finishing times. In R, an Exponential mean of 100 requires rate = 1/100, since its mean is the reciprocal of its rate.

set.seed(84735)
N_races <- 100000
go_time   <- rnorm(N_races, mean = 500, sd = 50) + rexp(N_races, rate = 1 / 100)
stop_time <- 250 + rnorm(N_races, mean = 200, sd = 30) + rexp(N_races, rate = 1 / 50)
stop_wins <- stop_time < go_time
p_stop <- mean(stop_wins)
c(estimate = p_stop, se = sd(stop_wins) / sqrt(N_races))
#>    estimate          se 
#> 0.811480000 0.001236858

Under these illustrative assumptions, the probability of stopping is approximately 81.1%, with Monte Carlo standard error 0.12 percentage points. We drew from the joint density of the two finishing times, which is easy because each is a sum of things R can draw, and averaged the indicator that the stop process won. We could just as easily estimate the mean finishing time of the winning process, the probability that a go response takes longer than 800 ms, or any other expectation, from the same draws. For each quantity, first specify the function to average and check that its expectation exists. The standard error concerns simulation under the chosen model, not uncertainty about whether the model is appropriate.

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.4 Generating draws from a distribution
So far, R has provided the required draws. In Bayesian analyses, however, the posterior distribution often does not belong to a familiar family with a built-in random generator. We therefore need methods for constructing draws. Inverse-transform sampling uses cumulative probabilities; rejection sampling uses the shape of a density. Both can produce independent draws when their inputs are independently generated.

1.4.1 Inverse-transform sampling
The cumulative distribution function (CDF), \(F(x)=P(X\le x)\), records how much probability lies to the left of \(x\). Its inverse, the quantile function, starts with a cumulative probability \(u\) and returns the corresponding value of \(x\). For a continuous, strictly increasing CDF, \(F^{-1}(u)\) is the value satisfying \(F(x)=u\).
Imagine choosing a height \(u\) uniformly between zero and one on a CDF plot. Move horizontally to the curve, then down to the \(x\) axis. The value you reach is a draw from the desired distribution. The left panel of Figure 1.5, below, shows five such constructions.
Formally, draw \(U\sim\text{Unif}(0,1)\) and set \(X=F^{-1}(U)\). Because \(F\) is increasing, the events \(F^{-1}(U)\le x\) and \(U\le F(x)\) are equivalent. Hence \[
P(X\le x)=P(F^{-1}(U)\le x)=P(U\le F(x))=F(x).
\] The last equality holds because a uniform draw falls below any number \(u\in[0,1]\) with probability \(u\). Thus the generated \(X\) has the desired CDF.
Take the Exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda\), which has \(F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x \geq 0\). To solve \(u=1-e^{-\lambda x}\), rearrange to \(1-u=e^{-\lambda x}\), take logarithms to get \(\log(1-u)=-\lambda x\), and divide by \(-\lambda\). This gives \(F^{-1}(u)=-\log(1-u)/\lambda\). So an Exponential draw is one line of code:

set.seed(84735)
r_exponential <- function(N, rate) -log(1 - runif(N)) / rate
draws_exp <- r_exponential(10000, rate = 2)


u_demo <- c(0.15, 0.4, 0.62, 0.8, 0.95)
x_demo <- -log(1 - u_demo) / 2
cdf_df <- tibble(x = seq(0, 3, length.out = 300), cdf = pexp(x, rate = 2))
paths <- tibble(u = u_demo, x = x_demo)

p_cdf <- ggplot(cdf_df, aes(x, cdf)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray50") +
  geom_segment(data = paths, aes(x = 0, xend = x, y = u, yend = u),
               color = "#552E6B", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_segment(data = paths, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = u, yend = 0),
               color = "#552E6B", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(data = paths, aes(0, u), color = "#552E6B") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "F(x)")

p_hist <- ggplot(tibble(x = draws_exp), aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, fill = "#ECECEC", color = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dexp, args = list(rate = 2), color = "#552E6B", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Density")

wrap_plots(p_cdf, p_hist)







Figure 1.5: Inverse-transform sampling for the Exponential(2) distribution. Left: five values of \(u\) (points on the vertical axis) are mapped through the inverse CDF to values \(x = F^{-1}(u)\) on the horizontal axis. Right: 10,000 draws produced this way, with the Exponential(2) density overlaid.





The histogram follows the Exponential density, and the simulated mean, 0.502, is close to \(1/\lambda=0.5\). This is one way to generate Exponential draws; it is not the algorithm used internally by R’s rexp() see its documentation.
A numerical quantile function is sufficient; a closed-form inverse is not required. For example, qnorm(runif(1000)) generates standard Normal draws even though the Normal quantile function has no elementary formula. For a discrete distribution, use the smallest \(x\) for which \(F(x)\ge u\). This selects the appropriate step of its CDF.
The limitation is that we need \(F^{-1}\). For a posterior density we typically know only the shape, \(f(\theta \mid y) \propto f(y \mid \theta) f(\theta)\), and computing the CDF, let alone inverting it, requires exactly the integral we were trying to avoid.


1.4.2 Rejection sampling
Rejection sampling generates candidates from an accessible distribution and keeps some of them to obtain the distribution we want. Suppose we can evaluate the target density \(f(x)\), or even just a function \(h(x)\) that is proportional to it, \(f(x) = h(x)/Z\) with an unknown constant \(Z\). Suppose also that we have some other density \(q(x)\), called the proposal, that we can draw from, and a constant \(M\) such that \[
h(x) \le M\, q(x) \quad \text{for every } x.
\] The function \(M q(x)\) is an envelope. It lies at or above \(h\) everywhere. Rejection sampling draws a point uniformly under the envelope and keeps it if it also lies under \(h\).
For a uniform proposal on \([0,1]\), the envelope is a rectangle. A candidate’s horizontal position is uniform; its vertical position is uniform between zero and the envelope’s height. Where the target curve is high, a larger fraction of candidates lie below it and are kept. This makes accepted values more common in high-density regions. The left panel of Figure 1.6, below, shows the construction.


Rejection sampling

Given a target \(h(x) \propto f(x)\), a proposal density \(q\), and a constant \(M\) with \(h(x) \le M q(x)\) for all \(x\):

Propose. Draw \(x^\star \sim q\).
Accept or reject. Draw \(u \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)\). If \(u < h(x^\star) / (M q(x^\star))\), accept \(x^\star\); otherwise reject it and return to step 1.

The accepted values are independent draws from \(f\). The probability that a proposal is accepted is \(Z/M\) when \(q\) is a proper density, where \(Z = \int h(x)\,dx\).

Why does this produce draws from \(f\)? A proposal at \(x\) is accepted with probability \(h(x)/(M q(x))\), so the density of proposing \(x\) and accepting it is \[
q(x) \cdot \frac{h(x)}{M q(x)} = \frac{h(x)}{M}.
\] This is a joint density for the candidate value together with acceptance, not yet the density among accepted values. Its integral is the probability of acceptance, \[
P(\text{accept})=\int\frac{h(x)}{M}\,dx=\frac{Z}{M}.
\] To obtain the conditional density among accepted values, divide by that probability: \[
f(x\mid\text{accept})=\frac{h(x)/M}{Z/M}=\frac{h(x)}{Z}=f(x).
\] This explains why the unknown normalizing constant \(Z\) is not needed to run the algorithm. The acceptance step corrects the relative frequencies of the proposed values.
For a fixed proposal \(q\), we want the smallest valid \(M\). Increasing \(M\) enlarges the envelope without changing the area under \(h\), so the acceptance rate \(Z/M\) falls. Choosing \(M\) too small is different; it invalidates the sampler wherever \(h(x)>Mq(x)\).
We now return to using \(\pi\) for an on-time probability. Apply rejection sampling to the function \(h(\pi) = \pi^{18}(1 - \pi)^{7}\) on the interval \([0, 1]\). A function proportional to a density is called its kernel. This one is the kernel of a \(\text{Beta}(19,8)\) density, which gives us a known distribution against which to check the sampler. The simplest proposal is the uniform density on \([0, 1]\), \(q(\pi) = 1\), and the smallest valid \(M\) is then the maximum of \(h\), which is at \(\pi = 18/25\). Every proposal is a uniform point in the unit interval and is accepted with probability \(h(\pi^\star)/M\).

set.seed(84735)
h <- function(p) p^18 * (1 - p)^7
M <- h(18 / 25)

N_prop <- 20000
proposal <- runif(N_prop)
u <- runif(N_prop)
accept <- u < h(proposal) / M
draws_rej <- proposal[accept]
mean(accept)
#> [1] 0.2196


env_df <- tibble(proposal, u, accept) |> slice_head(n = 3000)
curve_h <- tibble(p = seq(0, 1, length.out = 400), scaled_h = h(p) / M)

p_env <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = env_df, aes(proposal, u, color = accept), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = curve_h, aes(p, scaled_h), color = "gray50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#552E6B", "FALSE" = "#ECECEC"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "u")

p_rej <- ggplot(tibble(p = draws_rej), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, fill = "#ECECEC", color = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dbeta, args = list(shape1 = 19, shape2 = 8), color = "#552E6B", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "Density")

wrap_plots(p_env, p_rej)







Figure 1.6: Rejection sampling for \(h(\pi) = \pi^{18}(1-\pi)^7\) with a uniform proposal. Left: the first 3,000 proposals, placed at height \(u\) under the flat envelope at 1, so that the target is drawn as \(h(\pi)/M\); points under the curve (purple) are accepted, the rest (gray) are rejected. Right: histogram of all accepted draws with the Beta(19, 8) density overlaid.





The left panel of Figure 1.6 shows how acceptance changes the distribution of candidates. The proposals fill the rectangle under the envelope uniformly; the accepted ones fill the region under the scaled target \(h/M\) uniformly; and a uniform scatter under a curve, projected onto the horizontal axis, has that curve as its density. The right panel provides a visual check that the 4,392 accepted draws follow the \(\text{Beta}(19, 8)\) density.
The price is the rejections. Only 22% of the proposals survived, close to the theoretical rate \(Z/M = B(19, 8)/M = 0.219\), where \(B(19,8)\) is the Beta function, the normalizing constant of \(h\). The acceptance rate is the ratio of the area under \(h\) to the area under the envelope; a tighter envelope wastes fewer proposals. Here the flat envelope is a poor fit to a peaked target, and about 78% of the proposals are thrown away. Whether this is affordable depends on how many accepted draws we need and how expensive each proposal is. With several parameters, a poorly fitting envelope can become much more wasteful.
Products of many small likelihood terms can underflow, meaning the computer rounds them to zero. To avoid this, compute log densities directly and compare log(u) with log_h(proposal) - log_M. Taking log(h(proposal)) after an underflow has occurred cannot recover the lost value. Chapter 2 develops calculations on the log scale.
The Metropolis algorithm in Chapter 5 also proposes a value and then accepts or rejects it. Its acceptance rule is different and depends on the current state. We will derive that rule separately.


Quiz yourself!

Suppose you had used \(M = 2\,h(18/25)\) instead of \(M = h(18/25)\), an envelope twice as high as necessary. What happens to the acceptance rate? What happens to the distribution of the accepted draws? And what if you had used \(M = h(18/25)/2\)?

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.5 Simulating a Bayesian model forward
Sara records 12 on-time arrivals among 15 trains. Conditional on \(\pi\), we model the count as \(Y\mid\pi\sim\text{Bin}(15,\pi)\). A Binomial distribution describes the number of successes in independent trials with a common success probability. Its probability mass at 12 is \[
P(Y=12\mid\pi)=\binom{15}{12}\pi^{12}(1-\pi)^3.
\] The coefficient counts the arrangements of 12 on-time and three late arrivals. With the observed count fixed, this expression is the likelihood, viewed as a function of \(\pi\).
Bayes’ rule updates the prior by multiplying it by the likelihood and then normalizing. The Beta\((7,5)\) prior has kernel \(\pi^6(1-\pi)^4\), so \[
f(\pi\mid Y=12)\propto
\underbrace{\pi^{12}(1-\pi)^3}_{\text{likelihood kernel}}
\underbrace{\pi^6(1-\pi)^4}_{\text{prior kernel}}
=\pi^{18}(1-\pi)^7.
\] This is the Beta\((19,8)\) kernel used in the rejection-sampling example. The posterior distribution represents Sara’s uncertainty after observing the data. Chapter 2 develops Bayesian updating further.
We can also obtain this posterior by simulation. First draw a possible on-time probability from the prior, then generate a count using that value. Repeating these steps gives pairs \((\pi^{(s)},Y^{(s)})\), where \(s\) indexes simulations. Their joint distribution is \(f(\pi)f(y\mid\pi)\). The distribution of the simulated counts alone is the prior predictive distribution; it describes data predicted before observing Sara’s record.
Now retain only pairs whose simulated count is 12. Within those pairs, the distribution of \(\pi\) is the conditional distribution given \(Y=12\), which is precisely the posterior. Each entry of pi_prior below is used to generate one corresponding entry of y_sim; the logical condition selects the matching parameter draws.

set.seed(84735)
N_sim <- 100000
pi_prior <- rbeta(N_sim, shape1 = 7, shape2 = 5)          # 1. draw pi from the prior
y_sim    <- rbinom(N_sim, size = 15, prob = pi_prior)      # 2. simulate a week of trains
pi_post  <- pi_prior[y_sim == 12]                          # 3. keep the weeks that match
length(pi_post)
#> [1] 8358


joint <- tibble(pi = pi_prior, y = y_sim, keep = y_sim == 12)

p_joint <- joint |>
  slice_head(n = 5000) |>
  ggplot(aes(pi, y, color = keep)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(height = 0.25, width = 0, seed = 1),
             size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#552E6B", "FALSE" = "#ECECEC"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 15, 3)) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "Simulated Y")

p_post <- ggplot(tibble(pi = pi_post), aes(pi)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, fill = "#ECECEC", color = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dbeta, args = list(shape1 = 19, shape2 = 8), color = "#552E6B", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "Density")

wrap_plots(p_joint, p_post)







Figure 1.7: Forward simulation of the Beta-Binomial model. Left: 5,000 of the simulated \((\pi, Y)\) pairs from the joint distribution of parameter and data; the pairs with \(Y = 12\), the observed value, are purple. Right: histogram of all retained draws of \(\pi\) with the exact Beta(19, 8) posterior overlaid.





The left panel of Figure 1.7 shows the joint distribution. Small \(\pi\) produces small \(Y\), large \(\pi\) produces large \(Y\), and the purple row is the slice at \(Y = 12\). The right panel shows that the \(\pi\) values in that slice are distributed as \(\text{Beta}(19, 8)\). Their summaries agree with the exact posterior as well:

c(mean = mean(pi_post), sd = sd(pi_post),
  lower = quantile(pi_post, 0.025, names = FALSE), upper = quantile(pi_post, 0.975, names = FALSE))
#>       mean         sd      lower      upper 
#> 0.70253618 0.08615037 0.52149758 0.85547385
c(mean = 19 / 27, sd = sqrt(19 * 8 / (27^2 * 28)), lower = qbeta(0.025, 19, 8), upper = qbeta(0.975, 19, 8))
#>       mean         sd      lower      upper 
#> 0.70370370 0.08629368 0.52212521 0.85674000

The retained draws describe uncertainty about \(\pi\). Their standard deviation is a posterior standard deviation; the interval between their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles is a 95% equal-tailed credible interval. The Monte Carlo standard error of the estimated posterior mean is a different quantity, estimated by sd(pi_post) / sqrt(length(pi_post)). More simulations reduce that computational error without changing the posterior itself.
The link to rejection sampling follows by considering the probability of keeping a proposed \(\pi^\star\). It is \(P(Y=12\mid\pi^\star)\), since that is the probability that the simulated count matches the observed one. This value is at most one because \(Y\) is discrete and we use its full probability mass, including the Binomial coefficient. A likelihood in general is not a probability distribution over the parameter, and a continuous-data likelihood is not bounded by one.
With proposal \(q(\pi)=f(\pi)\) and unnormalized target \(h(\pi)=f(12\mid\pi)f(\pi)\), we therefore have \(h(\pi)\le q(\pi)\). The rejection constant \(M=1\) is valid, and the acceptance ratio is \(h(\pi)/q(\pi)=f(12\mid\pi)\).


Forward simulation is rejection sampling

For discrete data, drawing \(\pi\) from the prior, simulating data, and keeping the draws whose simulated data equal the observed data \(y\) is rejection sampling with proposal \(q(\pi) = f(\pi)\), unnormalized target \(h(\pi)=f(\pi)f(y\mid\pi)\) using the full data probability mass, and \(M=1\). Its acceptance rate is \[
P(\text{keep}) = \int f(y \mid \pi) f(\pi)\,d\pi = f(y),
\] the prior predictive probability of the observed count, also called its marginal likelihood. Chapter 2 discusses this quantity further.

This calculation also reveals the computational cost. Only a fraction \(f(y)\) of simulations are retained. For the Beta-Binomial model, integrating the likelihood against the prior gives \[
f(y)=\binom{n}{y}\frac{B(7+y,5+n-y)}{B(7,5)},
\] where \(B(a,b)=\int_0^1 p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}\,dp\) is the Beta normalizing constant. The following function evaluates the expression on the log scale before converting it back to a probability. lchoose() and lbeta() return the logarithms of the Binomial coefficient and Beta function.

f_y <- function(y, n, a, b) {   # computed on the log scale to avoid overflow
  exp(lchoose(n, y) + lbeta(a + y, b + n - y) - lbeta(a, b))
}
f_y(12, n = 15, a = 7, b = 5)
#> [1] 0.08409611

The calculation predicts the acceptance rate; about 8% of the simulated records were retained in our run. Now suppose Sara keeps going. Consider longer records with 120 of 150 and 1,200 of 1,500 trains on time. The observed proportion stays at 0.8. The chance that a simulated record matches hers exactly shrinks roughly in proportion to the number of trains. We reuse the prior draws in pi_prior, and the week already simulated in y_sim, and simulate the two longer records from the same prior draws:

set.seed(84735)
y_sim_150  <- rbinom(N_sim, size = 150,  prob = pi_prior)
y_sim_1500 <- rbinom(N_sim, size = 1500, prob = pi_prior)
survival <- tibble(
  n = c(15, 150, 1500), y = c(12, 120, 1200),
  predicted = f_y(y, n, a = 7, b = 5),
  survivors = c(sum(y_sim == 12), sum(y_sim_150 == 120), sum(y_sim_1500 == 1200))
)
survival
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>       n     y predicted survivors
#>   <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <int>
#> 1    15    12  0.0841        8358
#> 2   150   120  0.00686        668
#> 3  1500  1200  0.000650        68

For the largest record, 68 of 100,000 simulations reproduce the observed count. These are still valid posterior draws, but fewer retained values mean more Monte Carlo error. Whether they are sufficient depends on the summary and precision required. A small number might give a rough mean while providing little information about a small tail probability.
Matching additional observations can lower acceptance further, but the joint matching probability is a product of marginal probabilities only under independence. For continuous observations, the probability of an exact match is zero. Accepting values within a tolerance changes the target and requires additional justification.


Quiz yourself!

Sara’s colleague Joost keeps a longer record: 60 trains, 48 of them on time. Under the same \(\text{Beta}(7, 5)\) prior, roughly how many of 100,000 forward simulations will match his record? Use the function f_y() to find out, and explain why the answer is smaller than for Sara’s week.

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
section: 1.6 When independent draws are not enough
text:
1.6 When independent draws are not enough
Monte Carlo integration and sampling are separate tasks. If we can draw from the desired distribution, we can estimate many of its summaries by averaging. The difficulty is often obtaining those draws efficiently. Familiar distributions have built-in generators, and some others have accessible quantile functions or useful rejection envelopes. More complicated posteriors may have none of these conveniences.

1.6.1 One parameter: Using what we can evaluate
A posterior can often be evaluated up to a constant through \[
f(\theta\mid y)\propto f(y\mid\theta)f(\theta).
\] Here \(\theta\) denotes the unknown parameter or parameters, and \(y\) the fixed observed data. The right-hand side gives the posterior’s relative height at different values of \(\theta\), even when the integral needed to normalize it is difficult. This is enough for rejection sampling if we can find a suitable envelope. The Beta example showed the calculation in one dimension, where the target and envelope can be plotted directly.


1.6.2 Several parameters: Why a poor proposal becomes expensive
Consider a simple illustration with several parameters, each between zero and one. Suppose the target is uniform on the interval \([0.25,0.75]\) for each parameter, but our proposal draws every coordinate independently from \([0,1]\). A proposal is kept only if all its coordinates lie in the target intervals.
For one parameter, the acceptable interval occupies half the proposal range, so the acceptance probability is \(1/2\). For two parameters, both independent conditions must hold, giving \((1/2)(1/2)=1/4\). With \(d\) parameters, the acceptance rate is \((1/2)^d\).








Figure 1.8: A broad proposal with several parameters. Left: For two parameters the acceptable central square occupies one quarter of the proposal square. Right: Requiring all d independent coordinates to fall in their middle halves gives acceptance probability (1/2) to the power d. This illustrates a particular poor proposal, not a universal rate for high-dimensional sampling.





At ten parameters, about one in 1,024 proposals is accepted; at twenty, about one in a million. Each individual condition is easy to satisfy, yet satisfying all of them at once is unlikely. This example requires only multiplication of independent probabilities, rather than geometry in higher dimensions.
The problem is the mismatch between proposal and target. In this deliberately simple example, drawing each coordinate directly from \([0.25,0.75]\) solves it completely. For a real posterior, finding a proposal that matches both its concentration and the relationships between parameters can be much harder. Dimension alone does not force rejection sampling to fail, and dependent draws are not the only possible solution.
Markov chain Monte Carlo offers another approach. Instead of generating every candidate independently, we construct a sequence in which the next state depends on the current state. With an appropriate transition rule, long-run averages can estimate expectations under the target distribution. A Markov chain has the specific property that, conditional on the current state, its next state does not depend on the earlier history. Dependence alone does not ensure either this property or the desired long-run distribution.
A chain can use its current location to propose nearby values, but this does not guarantee efficient exploration. It may move slowly or remain in one region for a long time. Chapter 3 develops the conditions needed for these methods, and Chapter 4 explains how to assess their performance.

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.7 Chapter summary
This chapter introduced simulation as a way to calculate properties of probability models.

Expectations are probability-weighted sums, \(\sum_x g(x)f(x)\), or integrals, \(\int g(x)f(x)\,dx\). Means, variances, and event probabilities can be expressed this way when they exist.
Monte Carlo integration draws independently from the required distribution and averages \(g(X)\). The Law of Large Numbers establishes convergence when the absolute expectation is finite. With finite variance, the standard error is \(\text{sd}(g(X))/\sqrt{N}\). The rate does not explicitly depend on dimension, but the variance and difficulty of generating draws can.
Pseudo-random numbers come from a deterministic generator. Reproducibility requires the seed, code, generator settings, and software environment.
Inverse-transform sampling converts uniform draws into quantiles of the target distribution. A numerical quantile function can be sufficient.
Rejection sampling accepts a proposal from \(q\) with probability \(h(x)/(Mq(x))\). A valid envelope satisfies \(h(x)\le Mq(x)\) everywhere, and a tighter envelope improves acceptance for a fixed proposal.
Forward simulation generates parameters and data from their joint distribution. For discrete data, retaining exact matches gives posterior draws. The acceptance rate is the prior predictive probability of the observed data.
Poorly matched proposals can be expensive with many parameters. Markov chain Monte Carlo is one approach to this difficulty; its dependent draws require separate convergence and accuracy checks.

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.8 Quiz answers
Quiz 1. \(P(0.6 < \pi < 0.8) = E[g(\pi)]\) with \(g(\pi) = \mathbb{1}\{0.6 < \pi < 0.8\}\), the function that equals one inside the interval and zero outside it, and the expectation taken under the \(\text{Beta}(7, 5)\) prior. The Monte Carlo estimate is the proportion of prior draws that land in the interval.
Quiz 2. The standard error is proportional to \(1/\sqrt{N}\), so quadrupling \(N\) halves it. For a 95% interval of \(\pm 0.001\) we need \(2\sqrt{\pi(4-\pi)/N} \le 0.001\), which gives \(N \ge 4 \pi (4 - \pi) / 0.001^2 \approx 10.8\) million darts. Reducing the interval width by a factor of ten requires a hundred times as many draws with this estimator.
Quiz 3. With an envelope twice as high, each proposal is accepted with half the probability, so the acceptance rate halves from about 22% to about 11%. The distribution of the accepted draws does not change. The acceptance probability is still proportional to \(h\), and the constant cancels in the argument that the accepted draws have density \(f\). With \(M = h(18/25)/2\), the envelope lies below \(h\) near the mode, and the ratio \(h(\pi)/M\) exceeds one there, so every proposal near the mode is accepted; the peak is underrepresented relative to the tails, and the accepted draws have the wrong distribution. An envelope that is too low gives wrong answers; one that is too high only wastes time.
Quiz 4. The acceptance rate is the marginal likelihood f_y(48, n = 60, a = 7, b = 5) \(= 0.018\), so roughly 1,800 of 100,000 simulations match Joost’s record, against about 8,400 for Sara’s week. With more trains there are more possible values of \(Y\), and the prior probability of any one exact value is spread more thinly; the survival rate falls roughly in proportion to \(n\).

title: 1  Probability and Simulation
text:
1.9 Exercises

1.9.1 Conceptual exercises

Exercise 1.1 (Writing summaries as expectations) For each of the following quantities, write it as \(E[g(X)]\) for a suitable function \(g\), say what distribution \(X\) has, and write one line of R that estimates it from a vector x of draws.

\(P(X > 2)\) for \(X \sim \text{N}(0, 1)\).
The variance of a \(\text{Beta}(2, 5)\) variable.
The posterior probability that a proportion \(\pi\) exceeds 0.5, given draws from the posterior.
The posterior predictive probability that the next train is on time, given posterior draws of \(\pi\). Hint: Conditional on \(\pi\), the success probability is \(\pi\); average this over the posterior uncertainty.



Exercise 1.2 (Seeds and sequences) A student estimates the same posterior mean in two Monte Carlo runs with identical inputs. The function simulate_posterior(a, b, n, y) begins with set.seed(1). She averages the two estimates to reduce Monte Carlo error.

Explain what the seed inside the function does to the two runs.
Is the averaged estimate more precise than a single run? Why or why not?
Rewrite the workflow so that the two runs are independent but the whole analysis is still reproducible.



Exercise 1.3 (Envelopes) A rejection sampler for a target \(h(x)\) uses a proposal \(q\) and a constant \(M\).

Explain in one sentence why \(M q(x) \ge h(x)\) must hold for every \(x\), and what goes wrong if it fails on some interval.
The sampler accepts 4% of its proposals. Someone suggests using the accepted draws anyway, since “4% of a million is still 40,000 draws”. Is this a valid objection to the sampler’s correctness, to its efficiency, or to neither?
If you could choose a proposal \(q\) that is proportional to \(h\), what would \(M\) be, and what would the acceptance rate be?



Exercise 1.4 (Forward simulation as rejection sampling) Consider a model for counts, with a Gamma prior on the expected count \(\lambda\): \(\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(3, 1)\) and \(Y_i \mid \lambda \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, 6\), with observed data \(y = (2, 0, 4, 1, 3, 2)\). The Gamma parameters are shape and rate, so its density is \(f(\lambda)=\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}/2\) for \(\lambda>0\). Conditional on \(\lambda\), the six counts are independent and \(P(Y_i=k\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!\). In R, use rgamma(N, shape = 3, rate = 1) and rpois(N, lambda) to simulate these distributions.

Describe the forward simulation that produces draws from the posterior of \(\lambda\).
Identify the proposal, the target, and the acceptance probability of the equivalent rejection sampler.
Write down the acceptance rate as an integral. Would it be larger or smaller if the six observations were replaced by their sum, \(\sum y_i = 12\), observed as a single Poisson count with rate \(6\lambda\)? Explain.




1.9.2 Practical exercises

Exercise 1.5 (Two estimators of \(\pi\)) The darts estimate \(\pi/4\) as the proportion of uniform points under the curve \(y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}\). An alternative is to draw \(X \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)\) and average \(g(X) = \sqrt{1 - X^2}\), which also has expectation \(\pi/4\) (Hanada & Matsuura, 2022, Section 2.2).

Implement both estimators with \(N = 10{,}000\) and report each with its Monte Carlo standard error.
Repeat each estimator 500 times and compare the standard deviations of the two sets of estimates. Which estimator is more precise, and by what factor?
Explain the difference in terms of the variance of the two functions being averaged.



Exercise 1.6 (A distribution without a mean) This optional exercise examines why the finite-expectation condition matters. The standard Cauchy distribution has CDF \(F(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{\pi}\arctan(x)\).

Derive \(F^{-1}(u)\) and write a function that generates Cauchy draws from uniform draws. Check it against dcauchy() with a histogram, restricting the plot to \([-10, 10]\).
Plot the running mean of 100,000 draws against the number of draws. Compare with the running mean of 100,000 Normal draws. What do you see, and what does it say about the Law of Large Numbers?
The Cauchy distribution reappears in Chapter 5 as a prior. Would a Monte Carlo estimate of the median of your draws behave better than the mean? Try it.



Exercise 1.7 (The inhibition function) Return to the stop-signal race model of the chapter. The stop-signal delay was fixed at 250 ms. In an experiment it varies from trial to trial.

Write a function p_stop(ssd, N_races = 100000, stop_mean = 200) that returns the Monte Carlo estimate of the probability of stopping for a given delay, together with its standard error.
Evaluate it for delays from 0 to 500 ms in steps of 50 ms and plot the probability of successful stopping. The inhibition function is often plotted instead as the complementary probability of responding, so label your vertical axis explicitly.
Change the mean of the Normal component of the stop duration from 200 ms to 300 ms, keeping its standard deviation and Exponential component unchanged. Redraw the curve. Describe in words what a slower stop process does to the inhibition function.



Exercise 1.8 (Rejection sampling with a better envelope) The uniform envelope in Figure 1.6 wastes nearly four of every five proposals.

Use a \(\text{Beta}(2, 2)\) proposal instead. Find the smallest valid \(M\) numerically with optimize() applied to the ratio \(h(\pi)/q(\pi)\), and run the sampler.
Report the acceptance rate and compare the histogram of the accepted draws with the \(\text{Beta}(19, 8)\) density.
Try a \(\text{Beta}(15, 6)\) proposal. What acceptance rate do you get, and why is it so much better? What would happen with a \(\text{Beta}(25, 4)\) proposal, whose left tail near zero is thinner than the target’s? Examine the limiting ratio as \(\pi\to0\); a numerical maximum on a finite search interval is not a proof of a valid envelope.




1.9.3 Applied exercises

Exercise 1.9 (Believing in ghosts) The pulse_of_the_nation data in the bayesrules package record, for 1,000 American adults, whether they believe in ghosts (the ghosts variable). Let \(\pi\) be the population proportion who do, with prior \(\pi \sim \text{Beta}(2, 4)\).

Load data("pulse_of_the_nation", package = "bayesrules") and inspect table(pulse_of_the_nation$ghosts, useNA = "ifany") before coding the response. Keep respondents with a recorded yes/no answer, and document which value denotes belief. Take the first 30 eligible respondents as your data and count how many believe in ghosts. Use forward simulation with 100,000 prior draws to approximate the posterior of \(\pi\). Report the number of retained draws, the posterior mean, and a 95% interval, and compare them with the exact Beta posterior.
Now use all eligible respondents, reporting their actual number rather than assuming there are 1,000 complete responses. How many of 100,000 forward simulations match the observed count? Use f_y() from the chapter to predict this number before you run the simulation.
Sample the posterior for the full data by rejection sampling instead, with a uniform proposal and \(M\) equal to the maximum of the posterior kernel. Report the acceptance rate. Compare the retained sample sizes and Monte Carlo standard errors for the posterior mean. Explain the difference in efficiency and what the methods have in common. A low acceptance rate does not invalidate the retained draws. Compute the kernel and acceptance comparison on the log scale to avoid underflow.






Hanada, M., & Matsuura, S. (2022). MCMC from scratch: A practical introduction to Markov chain Monte Carlo. Springer.


Johnson, A. A., Ott, M. Q., & Dogucu, M. (2022). Bayes rules! An introduction to applied Bayesian modeling. CRC Press.


Logan, G. D., & Cowan, W. B. (1984). On the ability to inhibit thought and action: A theory of an act of control. Psychological Review, 91(3), 295–327. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.91.3.295

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.1 Prior, likelihood, posterior
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York holds work by artists from many generations. Suppose you want to estimate the proportion of artists in its collection who were born in 1965 or later, classified here as Generation X or younger. The moma_sample data in the bayesrules R package contain a random sample of 100 artists and a variable recording this classification. In Bayes Rules!, these data illustrate inference for an unknown proportion using a Beta prior, a Binomial likelihood, and a Beta posterior available in closed form (Johnson et al., 2022, Chapter 8).
This chapter examines the calculation behind that update. Bayes’ rule combines a prior and a likelihood, then divides by a normalizing constant to obtain a posterior distribution. For some models, we can identify the posterior as a familiar distribution. For others, we must approximate it. We will use both approaches to estimate the proportion, summarize its uncertainty, and compare models for the data.
For further background on Bayesian models and posterior summaries, see Bayes Rules! (Johnson et al., 2022, Chapters 3–5 and 8). Run the following setup before working through the examples. As in Chapter 1, \(n\) denotes the number of observed data points and \(N\) the number of Monte Carlo draws.
Let \(\theta\) denote an unknown parameter, or a vector of parameters, and let \(y\) denote the observed data. The prior density \(f(\theta)\) describes uncertainty before observing these data. The sampling model specifies the distribution of possible data given \(\theta\). With \(y\) fixed at its observed value, its probability mass or density \(f(y\mid\theta)\) is the likelihood, viewed as a function of \(\theta\). The posterior density \(f(\theta\mid y)\) describes uncertainty after observing \(y\). Bayes’ rule says that the posterior density is \[
f(\theta \mid y) = \frac{f(y \mid \theta)\, f(\theta)}{f(y)},
\qquad
f(y) = \int f(y \mid \theta)\, f(\theta)\, d\theta.
\tag{2.1}\] The numerator multiplies the likelihood by the prior. It assigns relatively large values to parameter values supported by both. The symbol \(\propto\) means “proportional to”, so we can write \[
f(\theta\mid y)\propto f(y\mid\theta)f(\theta).
\] The right-hand side is the unnormalized posterior. Its integral need not be one. Dividing it by its integral, \(f(y)\) in Equation 2.1, produces a density with total area one.
The data \(y\) are held fixed throughout this calculation, so \(f(y)\) is a single number rather than a function of \(\theta\). It is called the normalizing constant or marginal likelihood. For discrete data, it is the prior predictive probability of observing \(y\). For continuous data, it is a prior predictive density at \(y\), which can exceed one.
When we evaluate the posterior at two parameter values, this constant cancels in their ratio. This is useful when the likelihood and prior can be evaluated but the integral over \(\theta\) is difficult. We can then compare posterior heights without calculating the constant. Later in the chapter we will see why model comparison sometimes requires that constant, or an equivalent calculation.

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.1.1 The modern art example
Let’s set up the running example. Of the 100 sampled artists, 14 are Gen X or younger:

moma_sample |>
  count(genx)
#>    genx  n
#> 1 FALSE 86
#> 2  TRUE 14
y <- sum(moma_sample$genx)
n <- nrow(moma_sample)

We use a Binomial sampling model, \(Y\mid\pi\sim\text{Bin}(n,\pi)\), treating the classifications as independent observations with a common probability \(\pi\). We assign \(\pi\) a \(\text{Beta}(4,6)\) prior, with mean \(4/(4+6)=0.4\). This prior describes uncertainty about the proportion in the collection; it does not assert that the observed sample proportion will be exactly 0.4. Combining the Binomial likelihood and Beta prior gives \[
f(\pi \mid y) \propto \binom{n}{y} \pi^{y} (1 - \pi)^{n - y} \times \frac{\pi^{3} (1 - \pi)^{5}}{B(4, 6)}.
\]
The factor \(\binom{n}{y}\) is the Binomial coefficient, and \(B(4,6)\) normalizes the Beta prior. Both are constant with respect to \(\pi\). They affect the overall scale of the numerator but not which values of \(\pi\) have higher posterior density. We will visualize the prior, likelihood, and posterior in Figure 2.1 after identifying the posterior distribution.


2.1.2 The log-scale habit
For numerical calculations, we write a function that returns the logarithm of the unnormalized posterior: \[
\log f(\pi \mid y) = \log f(y \mid \pi) + \log f(\pi) + \text{constant}.
\] On the log scale the product becomes a sum, and R’s d* functions compute each term with log = TRUE:

log_posterior <- function(pi) {
  dbinom(y, size = n, prob = pi, log = TRUE) +   # log likelihood
    dbeta(pi, 4, 6, log = TRUE)                   # log prior
}
log_posterior(0.15)
#> [1] -2.49048
log_posterior(0.5)
#> [1] -30.31011

Throughout this book, log_posterior() returns the unnormalized log posterior, calculated as the log likelihood plus the log prior.
The two values returned above are negative for this particular calculation. Log densities need not always be negative, because densities can exceed one. To compare posterior heights, subtract the two log values and exponentiate: \[
\frac{f(0.15\mid y)}{f(0.5\mid y)}
=\exp\!\left[\texttt{log\_posterior}(0.15)-\texttt{log\_posterior}(0.5)\right].
\] The resulting ratio is approximately 1,200,000,000,000. It compares densities at two points; it is not a ratio of probabilities assigned to those individual points.
The log scale helps prevent numerical underflow. If we record each artist’s classification separately, the joint likelihood is a product of Bernoulli probabilities. For a hypothetical sample of 10,000 artists, with 1,400 classified as Gen X or younger, this product becomes too small for the computer to represent:

y_big <- rep(c(1, 0), times = c(1400, 8600))          # 10,000 artists, 14% Gen X
prod(dbinom(y_big, size = 1, prob = 0.2))              # raw scale
#> [1] 0
sum(dbinom(y_big, size = 1, prob = 0.2, log = TRUE))   # log scale
#> [1] -4172.248

On the raw scale the likelihood underflows to exactly zero, so a ratio of two such rounded likelihoods could become 0/0. On the log scale it is a sum of ten thousand moderate numbers, and the result remains representable. The same construction applies to other models. Add the log likelihood terms and the log prior terms, leaving out the posterior normalizing constant.


Bayes' rule, computationally

The posterior is \(f(\theta\mid y)=f(y\mid\theta)f(\theta)/f(y)\). In the models studied here, we can evaluate the likelihood and prior at a specified parameter value. Integrating their product may be much harder.

log_posterior(theta) returns the log likelihood plus the log prior.
Differences between its values give log ratios of posterior densities.
Its integral on the original scale equals \(f(y)\) only when the full likelihood and normalized prior have been retained. Dropping additional constants preserves the posterior’s shape but changes that integral.

Posterior sampling can use relative heights; model comparison requires careful treatment of constants.



Quiz yourself!

Two students calculate log_posterior() for the modern art data. One uses dbinom(y, n, pi, log = TRUE), which includes the binomial coefficient \(\log \binom{n}{y}\); the other writes the Bernoulli likelihood as y * log(pi) + (n - y) * log(1 - pi), which does not. Their functions return different numbers. Do they describe different posteriors?

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.2 Conjugate families and kernel recognition
A prior family is conjugate to a sampling model when updating with that model leaves the posterior in the same family. This lets us identify a normalized posterior without numerically integrating it.
To see this, collect the terms in the unnormalized log posterior that depend on the parameter. An additive term independent of the parameter can be represented by \(C\). Matching the remaining expression to the log density of a known family is called kernel recognition.
For the modern art data, the log likelihood and log prior combine as \[
\begin{aligned}
\log f(\pi\mid y)
&=y\log\pi+(n-y)\log(1-\pi)
  +3\log\pi+5\log(1-\pi)+C\\
&=(y+4-1)\log\pi+(n-y+6-1)\log(1-\pi)+C.
\end{aligned}
\] The Beta\((a,b)\) log density has the form \((a-1)\log\pi+(b-1)\log(1-\pi)-\log B(a,b)\). Comparing coefficients gives \[
\pi\mid y\sim\text{Beta}(y+4,n-y+6)
=\text{Beta}(18,92).
\] Thus the normalized posterior is available through R’s Beta functions. The Beta function \(B(y+4,n-y+6)\) normalizes the kernel \(\pi^{y+3}(1-\pi)^{n-y+5}\). The marginal likelihood of the original model also includes the constants from the likelihood and prior; we calculate it in the section on model comparison.
The three conjugate pairs in Table 2.1 can each be obtained by collecting terms in this way. The Gamma distribution uses shape and rate parameters; the second parameter of a Normal distribution in mathematical notation is its variance. In the Normal row, \(\theta\) and \(\tau^2\) are the prior mean and variance, \(\bar y\) is the sample mean, and \(\sigma^2\) is the known sampling variance. R’s dnorm() uses a standard deviation for its sd argument. Exercise 2.2 develops the Poisson and Normal cases.



Table 2.1: Three conjugate models. For repeated observations in the Poisson and Normal rows, observations are independent conditional on their parameter. The posterior parameters follow by adding the log likelihood and log prior and matching the resulting kernel.










Likelihood
Prior
Posterior




\(Y \mid \pi \sim \text{Bin}(n, \pi)\)
\(\pi \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)\)
\(\text{Beta}(\alpha + y,\; \beta + n - y)\)


\(Y_i \mid \lambda \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\)
\(\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(s, r)\)
\(\text{Gamma}(s + \sum_i y_i,\; r + n)\)


\(Y_i \mid \mu \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), \(\sigma\) known
\(\mu \sim \text{N}(\theta, \tau^2)\)
\(\text{N}\!\left(\dfrac{\theta/\tau^2 + n\bar{y}/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2 + n/\sigma^2},\; \dfrac{1}{1/\tau^2 + n/\sigma^2}\right)\)






Appendix D works through each derivation step by step, including the completion of the square in the Normal case, and illustrates how the posterior parameters combine prior information with the data.
Figure 2.1 displays the Beta update. The code evaluates each curve on the same grid. To compare their shapes, the likelihood is rescaled to have area one as a function of \(\pi\); this plotting choice does not turn the likelihood into a prior or a posterior. The posterior combines the likelihood with the prior and is shifted slightly toward the prior mean.

pi_plot <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 501)
delta <- pi_plot[2] - pi_plot[1]
lik <- dbinom(y, n, pi_plot)

tibble(pi = pi_plot,
       prior = dbeta(pi_plot, 4, 6),
       likelihood = lik / sum(lik * delta),
       posterior = dbeta(pi_plot, y + 4, n - y + 6)) |>
  pivot_longer(-pi, names_to = "curve", values_to = "density") |>
  mutate(curve = factor(curve, levels = c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(pi, density, color = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(prior = "gray55", likelihood = "gray30", posterior = "#552E6B"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(prior = "dashed", likelihood = "dotted", posterior = "solid"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "Density")







Figure 2.1: The Beta(4, 6) prior, the Binomial likelihood of 14 Gen X artists out of 100 (scaled to integrate to one), and the Beta(18, 92) posterior for the proportion \(\pi\) of Gen X or younger artists.







Kernel recognition

To identify a conjugate posterior:

Add the log likelihood and log prior.
Collect terms involving the parameter and group all other terms into \(C\).
Match the result to a known log density and identify its parameters, as in the Beta derivation and Table 2.1.

If no familiar kernel is apparent, this recognition method has not supplied a closed-form posterior. Numerical integration or sampling may still be possible.

A different prior can produce a posterior outside the conjugate family. Suppose we place a Normal prior on the log-odds, \[
z=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi},\qquad z\sim\text{N}(-1.5,1^2).
\] The odds \(\pi/(1-\pi)\) compare success with failure. For \(\pi=0.2\), the odds are \(0.2/0.8=0.25\) and the log-odds are \(\log(0.25)\approx-1.39\). The log-odds transformation takes a probability in \((0,1)\) to a value anywhere on the real line. Its inverse is \(\pi=1/(1+e^{-z})\), implemented by plogis() in R; qlogis() maps in the other direction. The resulting distribution of \(\pi\) is called a logit-Normal distribution.
To express this prior as a density for \(\pi\), we must account for how intervals change under the transformation. A short interval of width \(d\pi\) corresponds to a log-odds interval of width approximately \(|dz/d\pi|d\pi\). Equal probabilities in these corresponding intervals require \[
f_\pi(\pi)=f_z\!\left(\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\right)
\left|\frac{dz}{d\pi}\right|,
\qquad
\frac{dz}{d\pi}=\frac{1}{\pi(1-\pi)}.
\] The derivative factor is the Jacobian for this one-dimensional transformation. On the log scale, it contributes \(-\log\pi-\log(1-\pi)\). The following function includes it and returns \(-\infty\) outside \((0,1)\), corresponding to zero posterior density there.

log_posterior_logitnormal <- function(pi) {
  lp <- rep(-Inf, length(pi))
  inside <- pi > 0 & pi < 1
  p <- pi[inside]
  lp[inside] <- dbinom(y, size = n, prob = p, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(qlogis(p), mean = -1.5, sd = 1, log = TRUE) -
    log(p) - log1p(-p)
  lp
}

The function evaluates a log posterior even though the result does not have the Beta log-density form. In the grid section, we use these evaluations to approximate its normalized posterior.

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.3 Summarizing a posterior
A posterior distribution supports several kinds of summary. Means and interval probabilities are expectations, as in Chapter 1. Quantiles locate values below which specified amounts of posterior probability lie. The mode identifies the highest point of the density.



Table 2.2: Posterior summaries. Means and interval probabilities can be estimated by averaging functions of the draws. Credible interval endpoints are estimated by sample quantiles.










Summary
Definition
From posterior draws in theta




Mean
\(E[\theta\mid y]=\int\theta f(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta\)
mean(theta)


Variance
\(E[(\theta-E[\theta\mid y])^2\mid y]\)
var(theta)


Interval probability
\(P(a<\theta<b\mid y)=E[\mathbb{1}\{a<\theta<b\}\mid y]\)
mean(theta > a & theta < b)


Central 95% credible interval
2.5th and 97.5th posterior percentiles
quantile(theta, c(.025, .975))


Mode
A value maximizing \(f(\theta\mid y)\)
Optimize a density or log density






The first four rows of Table 2.2 specify the mean, variance, interval probability, and central interval calculations used below. For the modern art model, we can compute these summaries directly from the Beta posterior and compare them with estimates from independent draws. The interval in the code below contains 95% of the posterior probability for \(\pi\); it describes uncertainty about the population proportion.

a <- y + 4
b <- n - y + 6

exact <- c(mean = a / (a + b),
           sd = sqrt(a * b / ((a + b)^2 * (a + b + 1))),
           lower = qbeta(0.025, a, b),
           upper = qbeta(0.975, a, b),
           p_below_0.2 = pbeta(0.2, a, b))
exact
#>        mean          sd       lower       upper p_below_0.2 
#>  0.16363636  0.03511365  0.10090844  0.23792856  0.84898556

Now estimate the same summaries from \(N=10{,}000\) independent posterior draws. R’s rbeta() generates them directly because the posterior is a Beta distribution.

set.seed(84735)
N <- 10000
draws <- tibble(pi = rbeta(N, a, b))

draws |>
  summarize(mean = mean(pi), sd = sd(pi),
            lower = quantile(pi, 0.025), upper = quantile(pi, 0.975),
            p_below_0.2 = mean(pi < 0.2))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>    mean     sd lower upper p_below_0.2
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 0.164 0.0353 0.100 0.239       0.845

The simulated summaries are close to the exact values, but they vary from run to run. The Monte Carlo standard error of the mean is estimated by sd(draws$pi) / sqrt(N). For the estimated probability \(\hat p=\texttt{mean(draws\$pi < 0.2)}\), use \(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/N}\):

p_hat <- mean(draws$pi < 0.2)
c(mean_mcse = sd(draws$pi) / sqrt(N),
  probability_mcse = sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / N))
#>        mean_mcse probability_mcse 
#>     0.0003532832     0.0036161846

These errors concern the computation of posterior summaries. Increasing \(N\) reduces them without making the underlying posterior distribution narrower. The \(1/\sqrt{N}\) standard-error formula applies to independent averages with finite variance. Quantiles have their own sampling errors; their standard errors are not obtained by substituting a quantile into the formula for a mean.

2.3.1 Credible intervals and the mode
A central 95% credible interval leaves 2.5% of the posterior probability in each tail. Another choice is the highest posterior density (HPD) region, which contains 95% probability using values of highest density. For a continuous, unimodal density such as this Beta posterior, the HPD region is a shortest 95% interval. For a multimodal density, an HPD region can consist of separate intervals.
For the unimodal case, we can approximate a shortest interval from the draws. Sort them, consider every consecutive group containing at least 95% of the draws, and retain the narrowest group. The function below uses ceiling() to determine the required number of draws. Because it searches a finite sample, the result has Monte Carlo error.

hpd <- function(x, level = 0.95) {
  x <- sort(x)
  n_draws <- length(x)
  m <- ceiling(level * n_draws)
  stopifnot(level > 0, level < 1, m >= 2, m <= n_draws)
  starts <- seq_len(n_draws - m + 1)
  ends <- starts + m - 1
  i <- which.min(x[ends] - x[starts])
  c(lower = x[starts[i]], upper = x[ends[i]])
}
central_interval <- setNames(quantile(draws$pi, c(0.025, 0.975)),
                             c("lower", "upper"))
hpd_interval <- hpd(draws$pi)
rbind(central = central_interval, shortest = hpd_interval)
#>               lower     upper
#> central  0.10005397 0.2386363
#> shortest 0.09721451 0.2337647

To display the population intervals without sampling noise, the next figure obtains the shortest interval directly from the Beta quantile function. If \(q\) is the probability below its lower endpoint, then the upper endpoint has cumulative probability \(q+0.95\). We choose \(q\) between zero and 0.05 to minimize their distance.

q_lower <- optimize(function(q) qbeta(q + 0.95, a, b) - qbeta(q, a, b),
                    interval = c(0, 0.05))$minimum
intervals <- tibble(
  interval = c("Central: Equal tail probabilities", "HPD: Shortest interval"),
  lower = c(qbeta(0.025, a, b), qbeta(q_lower, a, b)),
  upper = c(qbeta(0.975, a, b), qbeta(q_lower + 0.95, a, b))
)
intervals |> mutate(width = upper - lower)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   interval                           lower upper width
#>   <chr>                              <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
