#> 1 Central: Equal tail probabilities 0.101  0.238 0.137
#> 2 HPD: Shortest interval            0.0973 0.233 0.136









Figure 2.2: Two 95% credible intervals for the same Beta(18,92) posterior. Shading marks the probability inside each interval. The central interval leaves equal tail probabilities; the HPD interval is slightly shorter and leaves unequal tails. The dotted vertical line marks the posterior mode, a point rather than an interval.





Both intervals in Figure 2.2 describe uncertainty about the same proportion. They differ because they use different rules to allocate the 5% probability left outside. The posterior mode, also called the maximum a posteriori estimate, is the value at the peak. It is a maximization, rather than an expectation or a quantile. For this model, it can be found directly:

mode_pi <- optimize(log_posterior, interval = c(0.001, 0.999), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
c(mode = mode_pi, mean = a / (a + b))
#>      mode      mean 
#> 0.1574135 0.1636364

For a continuous posterior, repeated draws almost never have identical values. Counting the most frequent draw therefore does not provide a useful way to estimate the mode.


Quiz yourself!

The museum’s benchmark is a Gen X share between 0.15 and 0.25. Write \(P(0.15 < \pi < 0.25 \mid y)\) as an expectation. How would you estimate it from the 10,000 draws in draws, and roughly how large is the Monte Carlo error of that estimate?

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
section: 2.4 Comparing models: marginal likelihoods and Bayes factors
text:
2.4 Comparing models: marginal likelihoods and Bayes factors
So far we have calculated probabilities for ranges of \(\pi\) within one model, such as \(\pi<0.2\) or \(0.15<\pi<0.25\). For illustration, suppose the museum’s board asks whether a model fixing the proportion at exactly 20% predicts the data better than a model allowing the proportion to vary. Under our continuous Beta posterior, \(P(\pi=0.2\mid y)=0\), just as it is for every other single value. Assessing a model that assigns all its parameter probability to 0.2 therefore requires a separate model comparison.


Interval and point hypotheses

An interval hypothesis says that the parameter lies in a range, such as \(\pi < 0.2\) or \(0.15 < \pi < 0.25\). Its posterior probability is an expectation and is computed as in the previous section. A point hypothesis specifies a single value, such as \(\pi=0.2\). A separate point-null model assigns its parameter probability to that value; its posterior model probability comes from comparing it with an alternative model.

We compare two models for the data: \(H_0\), in which \(\pi\) is fixed at \(0.2\), and \(H_1\), in which \(\pi\) is unknown and has the \(\text{Beta}(4, 6)\) prior. Each model makes a prediction about the data, and the prediction is its marginal likelihood, the very normalizing constant we have been avoiding: \[
f(y \mid H_0) = f(y \mid \pi = 0.2),
\qquad
f(y \mid H_1) = \int_0^1 f(y \mid \pi)\, f(\pi \mid H_1)\, d\pi.
\] Under \(H_0\) there is nothing to integrate, because \(\pi\) is fixed. Under \(H_1\), the marginal likelihood averages the likelihood over the prior. It is the prior predictive probability of the observed count, allowing for the uncertainty about \(\pi\) specified by that model. The Bayes factor is the ratio of the two, \[
\text{BF}_{01} = \frac{f(y \mid H_0)}{f(y \mid H_1)},
\tag{2.2}\] where the subscript \(01\) specifies the direction of comparison. \(\text{BF}_{01}>1\) favors \(H_0\) relative to \(H_1\); \(\text{BF}_{01}<1\) favors \(H_1\). The reverse comparison is \(\text{BF}_{10}=1/\text{BF}_{01}\).
The Bayes factor also describes how the data update model odds. Odds compare probabilities by division; for example, probabilities 0.75 and 0.25 give odds of \(3:1\). Applying Bayes’ rule to the models gives \[
\frac{P(H_0 \mid y)}{P(H_1 \mid y)} = \frac{f(y \mid H_0)}{f(y \mid H_1)} \times \frac{P(H_0)}{P(H_1)},
\tag{2.3}\] Thus posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by the Bayes factor. If the prior odds are \(1:1\) and \(\text{BF}_{01}=4\), the posterior odds are \(4:1\), giving \(P(H_0\mid y)=4/(4+1)=0.8\). With prior odds \(1:4\), the same Bayes factor instead gives posterior odds \(1:1\) and \(P(H_0\mid y)=0.5\).
For two models with prior model probabilities that sum to one, write \(O_{01}=P(H_0)/P(H_1)\). Then \[
P(H_0\mid y)=\frac{\text{BF}_{01}O_{01}}{1+\text{BF}_{01}O_{01}}.
\] These prior probabilities concern which model is considered plausible; they are distinct from the Beta prior on \(\pi\) within \(H_1\). Chapter 9 (Bayesian Variable Selection) and Chapter 10 (Bayesian Model Averaging) extend this reasoning to larger sets of models.
For the Beta-Binomial model both marginal likelihoods are available in closed form. Under \(H_1\) the integral is the same Beta-function integral that kernel recognition handled for us, \[
f(y \mid H_1) = \binom{n}{y} \frac{B(y + \alpha,\; n - y + \beta)}{B(\alpha, \beta)},
\] so we can compute the Bayes factor directly. We also compute the integral numerically with integrate(), to make the phrase “average the likelihood over the prior” concrete.

pi0 <- 0.2
ml_H0 <- dbinom(y, size = n, prob = pi0)
log_ml_H0 <- dbinom(y, size = n, prob = pi0, log = TRUE)
log_ml_H1 <- lchoose(n, y) + lbeta(y + 4, n - y + 6) - lbeta(4, 6)
ml_H1 <- exp(log_ml_H1)
ml_H1_numeric <- integrate(function(pi) dbinom(y, n, pi) * dbeta(pi, 4, 6), 0, 1)$value

c(ml_H0 = ml_H0, ml_H1 = ml_H1, ml_H1_numeric = ml_H1_numeric)
#>         ml_H0         ml_H1 ml_H1_numeric 
#>   0.033531484   0.007417289   0.007417289
BF_01 <- exp(log_ml_H0 - log_ml_H1)
BF_01
#> [1] 4.520719

The data are about 4.5 times more likely under \(H_0\) than under \(H_1\). With equal prior model probabilities, the posterior probability of the fixed-proportion model is \(P(H_0 \mid y) =\) 0.82.


Interpreting a Bayes factor

A Bayes factor is a continuous measure of evidence and its interpretation depends on the context. The ranges below provide a conventional descriptive vocabulary. Values close to a boundary, such as 2.9 and 3.1, represent similar evidence and should not lead to sharply different conclusions. Report the numerical Bayes factor, the compared models, and their priors.



\(\text{BF}_{10}\)
Evidence




\(> 10\)
strong for \(H_1\)


\(3\) to \(10\)
moderate for \(H_1\)


\(1\) to \(3\)
anecdotal for \(H_1\)


\(1\)
none


\(1/3\) to \(1\)
anecdotal for \(H_0\)


\(1/10\) to \(1/3\)
moderate for \(H_0\)


\(< 1/10\)
strong for \(H_0\)



Note that \(\text{BF}_{01} = 1 / \text{BF}_{10}\); a \(\text{BF}_{01}\) of 4.5 is a \(\text{BF}_{10}\) of about \(0.22\).

The categories follow Jeffreys (1961) as tabulated by Lee & Wagenmakers (2013).

2.4.1 The Savage–Dickey density ratio
In the modern art example, conjugacy makes both marginal likelihoods available. For more complicated models, integrating the likelihood over the prior can be difficult. In certain nested point-null comparisons, the Savage–Dickey density ratio instead calculates the Bayes factor from prior and posterior densities under the alternative. It requires matching sampling models at the null value and compatible priors, as specified in the box below (Dickey & Lientz, 1970; Wagenmakers et al., 2010).
For the one-parameter comparison here, the identity follows directly from Bayes’ rule. Under \(H_1\), Bayes’ rule evaluated at the null value \(\pi_0\) reads \[
f(\pi_0 \mid y, H_1) = \frac{f(y \mid \pi_0)\, f(\pi_0 \mid H_1)}{f(y \mid H_1)}.
\] Because \(H_0\) is nested in \(H_1\), the likelihood at \(\pi_0\) under \(H_1\) is the likelihood under \(H_0\): \(f(y \mid \pi_0) = f(y \mid H_0)\). Rearranging, \[
\text{BF}_{01} = \frac{f(y \mid H_0)}{f(y \mid H_1)} = \frac{f(\pi_0 \mid y, H_1)}{f(\pi_0 \mid H_1)}.
\tag{2.4}\] The Bayes factor for the point hypothesis is the posterior density at the null value divided by the prior density at the null value, both under \(H_1\). The ratio avoids separately computing the two marginal likelihoods. If the data make \(\pi_0\) more plausible than it was, the posterior density there exceeds the prior density and the Bayes factor favors \(H_0\); if the data pull the posterior away from \(\pi_0\), the Bayes factor favors \(H_1\).

prior_at_pi0 <- dbeta(pi0, 4, 6)
posterior_at_pi0 <- dbeta(pi0, y + 4, n - y + 6)
posterior_at_pi0 / prior_at_pi0
#> [1] 4.520719

The ratio agrees with the marginal-likelihood calculation. Figure 2.3 shows the two heights being compared. Both are densities under \(H_1\); neither is the probability that \(\pi\) is exactly 0.2.








Figure 2.3: Savage–Dickey for the modern art data. At the null value 0.2 (vertical dotted line), the posterior height is divided by the prior height. The resulting \(\text{BF}_{01}\) is printed on the plot. The calculation compares two model predictions; it does not assign point probability within the continuous posterior.







The Savage–Dickey density ratio

For the one-parameter comparison above, \(H_0\) fixes \(\theta=\theta_0\) and uses the same sampling model as \(H_1\) at that value. With a proper prior under \(H_1\) whose density is continuous and positive at \(\theta_0\), \[
\text{BF}_{01} = \frac{f(\theta_0 \mid y, H_1)}{f(\theta_0 \mid H_1)}.
\] The Bayes factor is the ratio of posterior to prior density at the null value, as in Equation 2.4. If the models also contain other parameters, their prior under \(H_0\) must match the conditional prior under \(H_1\) given \(\theta=\theta_0\). The ratio cannot be used for an arbitrary pair of nested models without checking this condition (Wagenmakers et al., 2010).



2.4.2 The prior matters
The alternative model includes a prior, so changing that prior changes its predictions and can change the Bayes factor. Compare the original Beta\((4,6)\) prior with Beta\((0.5,0.5)\), which places substantial mass near zero and one, and Beta\((20,80)\), which concentrates around 0.2. Each comparison uses the same point-null model and the same data.

priors <- tribble(
  ~prior,            ~alpha, ~beta,
  "Beta(0.5, 0.5)",     0.5,   0.5,
  "Beta(4, 6)",           4,     6,
  "Beta(20, 80)",        20,    80
)

sd_table <- priors |>
  mutate(prior_density = dbeta(pi0, alpha, beta),
         posterior_density = dbeta(pi0, alpha + y, beta + n - y),
         BF_01 = exp(dbeta(pi0, alpha + y, beta + n - y, log = TRUE) -
                     dbeta(pi0, alpha, beta, log = TRUE)))
sd_table
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   prior          alpha  beta prior_density posterior_density BF_01
#>   <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>             <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Beta(0.5, 0.5)   0.5   0.5         0.796              2.94 3.69 
#> 2 Beta(4, 6)       4     6           1.32               5.97 4.52 
#> 3 Beta(20, 80)    20    80           9.93               7.36 0.741


panels <- sd_table |>
  mutate(panel = paste0("'", prior, "'~~BF[\"01\"] == ", round(BF_01, 2)),
         panel = factor(panel, levels = panel))

curves <- panels |>
  select(panel, alpha, beta) |>
  crossing(pi = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 400)) |>
  mutate(prior = dbeta(pi, alpha, beta),
         posterior = dbeta(pi, alpha + y, beta + n - y)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(prior, posterior), names_to = "curve", values_to = "density")

dots <- panels |>
  select(panel, prior_density, posterior_density) |>
  pivot_longer(c(prior_density, posterior_density), names_to = "curve", values_to = "density") |>
  mutate(curve = if_else(curve == "prior_density", "prior", "posterior"))

ggplot(curves, aes(pi, density, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(color = "#552E6B") +
  geom_point(data = dots, aes(x = pi0, y = density), size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, labeller = label_parsed) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.6), ylim = c(0, 16)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(prior = "dashed", posterior = "solid"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "Density")







Figure 2.4: Prior (dashed) and posterior (solid) densities for \(\pi\) under three priors. The Savage–Dickey Bayes factor for \(\pi = 0.2\) is the ratio of the heights of the two dots. Under the diffuse prior the data raise the density at 0.2 a lot; under the concentrated prior they lower it slightly.





With Beta\((0.5,0.5)\) under \(H_1\), \(\text{BF}_{01}=3.69\); with Beta\((20,80)\), \(\text{BF}_{01}=0.74\). The observed sample proportion is 0.14. A model concentrated around 0.2 predicts these data differently from one spreading its mass across much of \([0,1]\). The values in Figure 2.4 therefore compare the fixed-proportion model with three distinct alternatives. Report the prior under \(H_1\) with the Bayes factor, and examine whether conclusions depend strongly on plausible changes to that prior.


2.4.3 Savage–Dickey from draws
The examples so far evaluate a Beta posterior density directly. When we have posterior draws instead, we can estimate that density at the null value and divide by the known prior density. This adds a density-estimation step. The following calculation illustrates it for a case where the exact answer is available; it is an optional numerical extension of the density-ratio identity.

set.seed(84735)
post_draws <- rbeta(1e5, y + 4, n - y + 6)
dens <- density(post_draws)
posterior_at_pi0_hat <- approx(dens$x, dens$y, xout = pi0)$y
posterior_at_pi0_hat / dbeta(pi0, 4, 6)
#> [1] 4.59112

Compare the estimate with the exact value 4.52. Unlike averaging an indicator, a kernel density estimate depends on a smoothing bandwidth. Estimating a density in a sparsely sampled tail can be unstable, and more draws do not remove the need to assess the smoothing choice. Use this calculation as a numerical check rather than assuming that any density estimate yields an accurate Bayes factor.


Quiz yourself!

A colleague reads that \(\text{BF}_{01} = 4.5\) for the board’s target of \(\pi = 0.2\) and concludes, “The posterior probability that \(\pi = 0.2\) is \(4.5/5.5 \approx 0.82\).” What is right about this and what is wrong?

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.5 Grid approximation and its limits
For the logit-Normal prior, we can evaluate the unnormalized log posterior but have not identified a familiar posterior family. A grid approximation divides a bounded parameter range into small cells and represents each cell by its midpoint. Multiplying the density at a midpoint by the cell width approximates the probability in that cell. We can normalize those approximate masses and then calculate summaries by summation.
This is a numerical approximation to a continuous distribution, rather than a claim that the parameter can take only the grid values. The grid must be fine enough to resolve the density and wide enough to include nearly all posterior probability.


Grid approximation

To approximate a one-dimensional posterior on a bounded interval:

Grid. Divide the interval into \(G\) equal cells of width \(\Delta\) and use their midpoints \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_G\).
Evaluate. For each grid index \(j=1,\ldots,G\), compute \(\ell_j=\log f(y\mid\theta_j)+\log f(\theta_j)\), using log_posterior(theta_j).
Normalize. Let \(c=\max_{j=1,\ldots,G}\ell_j\), set \(w_j=\exp(\ell_j-c)\), and calculate \(p_j=w_j/\sum_{k=1}^G w_k\).
Summarize. Approximate \(E[g(\theta)\mid y]\) by \(\sum_{j=1}^G g(\theta_j)p_j\), or sample midpoints with probabilities \(p_j\).

Here \(j\) and \(k\) index grid cells, and \(g\) is the function whose expectation we want. The weight \(p_j\) approximates the posterior probability in cell \(j\); \(p_j/\Delta\) approximates the density at its midpoint. Equal cell widths cancel when the weights are normalized. With unequal widths, each unnormalized weight must include its cell width.

Subtracting \(c\) before exponentiating changes all weights by the same factor, which cancels on normalization: \[
\frac{e^{\ell_j-c}}{\sum_k e^{\ell_k-c}}
=\frac{e^{-c}e^{\ell_j}}{e^{-c}\sum_k e^{\ell_k}}
=\frac{e^{\ell_j}}{\sum_k e^{\ell_k}}.
\] For example, the following raw exponentials all round to zero. After subtracting the maximum, the relative weights remain representable:

lp_demo <- c(-1001, -1000, -1002)
exp(lp_demo)
#> [1] 0 0 0
w_demo <- exp(lp_demo - max(lp_demo))
cbind(log_value = lp_demo, shifted_weight = w_demo,
      probability = w_demo / sum(w_demo))
#>      log_value shifted_weight probability
#> [1,]     -1001      0.3678794  0.24472847
#> [2,]     -1000      1.0000000  0.66524096
#> [3,]     -1002      0.1353353  0.09003057

At least one shifted weight is exactly one. Very small weights can still underflow, but they no longer cause every weight to become zero.
Here is the recipe as a function, followed by a check on the Beta prior, where we know the answer, and then the logit-Normal prior, where we do not.

grid_posterior <- function(log_posterior, grid, ...) {
  lp <- log_posterior(grid, ...)
  w <- exp(lp - max(lp))
  tibble(theta = grid,
         prob = w / sum(w),
         density = prob / (grid[2] - grid[1]))
}

G <- 200
pi_grid <- (seq_len(G) - 0.5) / G  # midpoints of G cells covering [0, 1]
grid_beta  <- grid_posterior(log_posterior, pi_grid)
grid_logit <- grid_posterior(log_posterior_logitnormal, pi_grid)


p_beta <- ggplot(grid_beta, aes(theta, density)) +
  stat_function(fun = dbeta, args = list(shape1 = y + 4, shape2 = n - y + 6),
                color = "#552E6B", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "Density", title = "Beta(4, 6) prior")

p_logit <- ggplot(grid_logit, aes(theta, density)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "Density", title = "Normal prior on the log-odds")

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_beta, p_logit)







Figure 2.5: Grid approximation with 200 points. Left: for the Beta(4, 6) prior the grid (dots) reproduces the exact Beta(18, 92) posterior (line). Right: the grid approximates the posterior under the Normal prior on the log-odds. Its accuracy must be assessed by refining the grid.





Posterior summaries follow from step 4 of the box. Here are the posterior mean and the probability that \(\pi < 0.2\) under both priors:

bind_rows(`Beta(4, 6)` = grid_beta, `logit-Normal` = grid_logit, .id = "prior") |>
  group_by(prior) |>
  summarize(mean = sum(theta * prob),
            p_below_0.2 = sum(prob[theta < 0.2]))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   prior         mean p_below_0.2
#>   <chr>        <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 Beta(4, 6)   0.164       0.849
#> 2 logit-Normal 0.143       0.945

The Beta row approximates the exact posterior mean of 0.164 with 200 evaluations of log_posterior(). Its probability estimate differs from the exact 0.849 by 1.8^{-4}. These are finite-cell approximations to integrals. Increasing the grid resolution provides a check on their accuracy. If a probability cutoff falls inside a cell, assigning that entire cell to one side introduces an additional approximation. When log_posterior() retains the full likelihood and normalized prior, the grid also approximates the marginal likelihood. On the log scale, the approximation is \(\log f(y)\approx c+\log(\Delta\sum_j w_j)\). Exercise 2.7 asks you to add this calculation. If the grid omits non-negligible posterior tails, normalizing over its cells instead approximates a truncated posterior.

2.5.1 Two parameters
Grid approximation extends to two parameters by gridding each and evaluating the log posterior at every combination. Consider a further question about the modern art data. Does the Gen X proportion differ between artists recorded as female and male? Restricting to the 99 artists who are recorded as female or male, we model \(Y_i \mid \pi_i \sim \text{Bern}(\pi_i)\) with \[
\log \frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{female}_i,
\qquad
\beta_0 \sim \text{N}(0, 2^2), \quad \beta_1 \sim \text{N}(0, 1^2).
\] Here \(i\) indexes artists, \(Y_i=1\) denotes Gen X or younger, and \(Y_i=0\) denotes an older generation. The Bernoulli distribution describes one such binary observation. The predictor \(\text{female}_i\) equals one for an artist recorded as female and zero for an artist recorded as male. This is a logistic regression with one binary predictor, and \(\beta_1\) is the log-odds ratio of being Gen X for female versus male artists. The model gives male artists probability \(\texttt{plogis}(\beta_0)\) and female artists probability \(\texttt{plogis}(\beta_0+\beta_1)\). Thus \(\beta_1>0\) means a larger modeled Gen X probability for female artists. The coefficient describes an association within the collection. The recorded gender categories determine which artists enter this illustration.
The independent Normal priors are not conjugate to this likelihood. We will approximate the joint posterior with a grid. Each row of grid_2d contains one combination of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), and map2_dbl() evaluates the log posterior at each combination.

art <- moma_sample |>
  filter(gender %in% c("female", "male")) |>
  mutate(genx = as.numeric(genx), female = as.numeric(gender == "female"))

log_posterior_2d <- function(beta0, beta1, data = art, sd_beta1 = 1) {
  eta <- beta0 + beta1 * data$female
  sum(dbinom(data$genx, size = 1, prob = plogis(eta), log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(beta0, 0, 2, log = TRUE) + dnorm(beta1, 0, sd_beta1, log = TRUE)
}

G <- 200
beta0_grid <- -6 + (seq_len(G) - 0.5) * 8 / G   # cells covering [-6, 2]
beta1_grid <- -6 + (seq_len(G) - 0.5) * 12 / G  # cells covering [-6, 6]
grid_2d <- expand_grid(beta0 = beta0_grid, beta1 = beta1_grid) |>
  mutate(lp = map2_dbl(beta0, beta1, log_posterior_2d),
         prob = exp(lp - max(lp)) / sum(exp(lp - max(lp))))


marginal_beta1 <- grid_2d |>
  group_by(beta1) |>
  summarize(prob = sum(prob))

p_joint <- ggplot(grid_2d, aes(beta0, beta1, fill = prob)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#552E6B", guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, -0.5), ylim = c(-1.5, 4)) +
  labs(x = expression(beta[0]), y = expression(beta[1]))

delta_beta1 <- diff(marginal_beta1$beta1)[1]
p_marg <- ggplot(marginal_beta1, aes(beta1, prob)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#552E6B", width = delta_beta1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.5, 4)) +
  labs(x = expression(beta[1]), y = "Posterior probability")

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_joint, p_marg)







Figure 2.6: Left: the joint posterior of the logistic regression intercept \(\beta_0\) and the gender effect \(\beta_1\) on a 200 by 200 grid; darker is more probable. Right: the marginal posterior of \(\beta_1\), obtained by summing the grid over \(\beta_0\). Both panels show a central portion of the wider evaluation grid.





To obtain a marginal posterior, sum over the parameter that is no longer of interest. In marginal_beta1, the weight for a given \(\beta_1\) adds the joint probabilities across all \(\beta_0\) cells. This is the grid counterpart of integrating out \(\beta_0\). The marginal posterior of \(\beta_1\) is the sum of the joint grid over \(\beta_0\), its mean is 1.26 on the log-odds scale, and the posterior probability that female artists are more likely to be Gen X, \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid y)\), is 0.987. Exercise 2.9 asks you to turn this grid into a Savage–Dickey Bayes factor for \(\beta_1 = 0\).


2.5.2 More parameters
Figure 2.7 shows how grid combinations multiply. With four values for one parameter, we evaluate four points. Adding a second parameter gives \(4\times4=16\) pairs; a third gives \(4\times4\times4=64\) triples. We evaluate every combination even if many have low posterior density.








Figure 2.7: Four midpoint values per parameter produce 4 points in one dimension, 16 pairs in two dimensions, and 64 triples in three dimensions. The three-dimensional grid is shown in projection. These points illustrate evaluation locations, not posterior draws.





Look at what the two-parameter grid cost: \(G^2 = 40,000\) evaluations of the log posterior, each a sum over 99 observations. Now count for a model with \(d\) parameters. A grid of \(G\) points per parameter has \(G^d\) points in total, and the number grows exponentially in \(d\).

expand_grid(d = 1:10, G = c(10, 50, 100)) |>
  mutate(points = G^d, G = factor(G, labels = paste("G =", c(10, 50, 100)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(d, points, color = G)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1e9, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("gray60", "gray30", "#552E6B"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Number of parameters d", y = "Grid points")







Figure 2.8: The number of grid points, \(G^d\), as a function of the number of parameters \(d\), for three grid resolutions. The vertical axis is logarithmic. The dashed line marks one billion evaluations.





With \(G = 100\) and \(d = 10\), a modest regression with an intercept, eight predictors, and a residual variance, the grid has \(10^{20}\) points. If the computer evaluates a million log posteriors per second, that is 3.2 million years. Dropping to \(G = 10\) brings it down to \(10^{10}\), a few hours, but ten points per parameter may miss important changes in a concentrated posterior density. Choosing a coarser grid saves work only if it still gives an adequate approximation.
A broad grid can also spend many evaluations in low-density regions. For the logistic regression, Figure 2.6 shows that the posterior occupies only part of the chosen rectangle. Narrowing the grid can save evaluations, but an overly narrow range discards posterior mass. Increasing the resolution addresses spacing; widening the range addresses truncation. Both require checks.
The growth from \(G\) to \(G^d\) points is one form of the curse of dimensionality. It concerns full grids at a fixed resolution per parameter. Adaptive integration and problem-specific structure can help, but a full grid becomes impractical for many models with several parameters.


Quiz yourself!

You want a grid with 50 points per parameter for a model with four parameters, and each evaluation of the log posterior takes one millisecond. How many evaluations are there, and how long will they take?

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.6 Sampling instead of gridding
In many models, we can evaluate an unnormalized posterior on the log scale even when we cannot integrate it. Grid approximation uses those evaluations to construct a discrete approximation, but its cost grows rapidly with the number of parameters. Sampling methods seek to obtain useful draws without evaluating every combination on a grid.
Markov chain Monte Carlo constructs dependent draws using a transition rule designed to have the posterior as its long-run distribution. In the Metropolis methods, the normalizing constant cancels in ratios of posterior heights, so a function such as log_posterior() supplies the needed evaluations. The transition rule and its conditions matter; an arbitrary sequence of accepted candidates need not represent the posterior. Chapter 3 develops those conditions, and Chapter 4 explains how to assess the resulting simulations.

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.7 Chapter summary
The chapter developed the connection between Bayesian updating and its numerical implementation.

Bayes’ rule normalizes the likelihood times the prior. The marginal likelihood \(f(y)\) is constant with respect to the parameter. log_posterior() evaluates the unnormalized log posterior; omitted constants must be tracked when calculating a marginal likelihood.
Kernel recognition identifies some posteriors by collecting parameter-dependent terms. Conjugate families supply familiar normalized posteriors; other models may require numerical methods.
Posterior summaries include expectations, quantiles, and modes. Posterior draws estimate them in different ways. A credible interval describes parameter uncertainty; Monte Carlo error describes numerical uncertainty in its estimated summaries.
Bayes factors compare marginal likelihoods and multiply prior model odds to obtain posterior model odds. Prior probabilities of models and priors on parameters within a model play different roles.
The Savage–Dickey density ratio compares posterior and prior density at a null value when its conditions hold. The densities are not point probabilities. Results depend on the specified alternative prior.
Grid approximation assigns weights to parameter cells and normalizes by summation. Subtracting the maximum log value stabilizes the calculation. Refining the spacing and checking the range address different approximation errors.
A full grid with \(G\) points for each of \(d\) parameters uses \(G^d\) evaluations. This motivates sampling methods that avoid enumerating every combination.

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.8 Quiz answers
Quiz 1. No. The two functions differ by \(\log \binom{n}{y}\), which does not depend on \(\pi\), and their normalized posteriors are identical. Normalizing either kernel gives the same posterior, because the extra constant cancels between the numerator and its integral. It would matter if the students wanted the marginal likelihood itself, because \(f(y)\) is the integral of the full likelihood times the prior, coefficient included.
Quiz 2. \(P(0.15 < \pi < 0.25 \mid y) = E[\mathbb{1}(0.15 < \pi < 0.25) \mid y]\), the expected value of an indicator. From draws it is mean(draws$pi > 0.15 & draws$pi < 0.25), which for the Beta(18, 92) posterior is about 0.61. The Monte Carlo standard error of a proportion \(p\) from \(N\) independent draws is \(\sqrt{p(1 - p)/N}\), estimated here by 0.0049.
Quiz 3. The arithmetic is right if two conditions hold: the prior probabilities of the two models are equal, so that \(P(H_0 \mid y) = \text{BF}_{01} / (1 + \text{BF}_{01})\), and “the probability that \(\pi = 0.2\)” is understood as the posterior probability of the model \(H_0\). What is wrong is reading it as a statement about the continuous posterior of \(\pi\) under \(H_1\), where \(P(\pi = 0.2 \mid y) = 0\) regardless of the data. The value 0.82 is a posterior model probability. It assumes a prior probability of one half for \(H_0\), which is additional to the Bayes-factor calculation.
Quiz 4. \(50^4 = 6{,}250{,}000\) evaluations. At one millisecond each, that is \(6{,}250\) seconds, about \(1.7\) hours. Adding a fifth parameter multiplies both numbers by 50.

title: 2  Bayesian Inference, Revisited
text:
2.9 Exercises

2.9.1 Conceptual exercises

Exercise 2.1 (Where did the constant go?) Explain, in words and in one formula, why we can compute posterior means, credible intervals, and posterior probabilities of interval hypotheses without ever evaluating \(f(y)\), provided we can draw from the posterior. Then explain why the absolute scale matters for a marginal likelihood, and why an ordinary posterior sample average does not directly give it. How does the Savage–Dickey identity allow certain Bayes factors to be calculated without separately evaluating marginal likelihoods?


Exercise 2.2 (Kernel recognition) Derive the second and third rows of Table 2.1 by kernel recognition.

For \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n \mid \lambda \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\) and \(\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(s, r)\), write the prior kernel and the joint likelihood kernel, multiply them, and identify the posterior.
For \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n \mid \mu \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known and \(\mu \sim \text{N}(\theta, \tau^2)\), do the same. Hint: expand the squares in the exponent, collect the terms in \(\mu^2\) and in \(\mu\), and complete the square.
Now replace the prior in (a) by \(\log \lambda \sim \text{N}(0, 1)\). Show that step 3 of the kernel recognition box fails, and write the log_posterior(lambda) function for this model anyway.



Exercise 2.3 (Point hypotheses, revisited) A fellow student has just learned about Bayes factors and has questions. Answer each in two or three sentences.

What is a point hypothesis, and why can its posterior probability not be read off the posterior distribution of the parameter?
What is an interval hypothesis, and how is its posterior probability an expectation?
What is a marginal likelihood, and why is it sometimes called the normalizing constant and sometimes the evidence?
What is the Savage–Dickey density ratio, when can it be used, and what does it avoid computing?
Why does a Bayes factor of 4.5 in favor of \(H_0\) not by itself mean that \(P(H_0 \mid y) = 0.82\)?



Exercise 2.4 (The prior matters, a lot) A well-being score is modeled as \(Y_i\mid\mu\sim\text{N}(\mu,0.5^2)\), independently for \(i=1,\ldots,25\). The observed mean is \(\bar y=5.735\). Compare \(H_0\!: \mu=6\) with \(H_1\!: \mu\sim\text{N}(6.5,\tau^2)\). Use the Normal posterior formula in Table 2.1 to explore how the Bayes factor changes as \(\tau\) grows.

Without computing, reason about what happens to the prior density at \(\mu = 6\) and to the posterior density at \(\mu = 6\) as \(\tau \to \infty\). What does this imply for \(\text{BF}_{01}\)?
Verify your reasoning with dnorm() for \(\tau \in \{0.4, 1, 5, 25, 100\}\).
This limit illustrates Bartlett’s paradox: With fixed data, spreading the alternative prior increasingly widely can favor the point null. Explain this using the prior predictive distribution, and discuss why increasing the prior variance is not a neutral choice for model comparison.




2.9.2 Practical exercises

Exercise 2.5 (Hypothesis tests, three ways) A colleague’s model for a mean \(\mu\) had a \(\text{N}(10, 10^2)\) prior and, after seeing the data, a \(\text{N}(5, 3^2)\) posterior.

Compute the posterior probability of the interval hypothesis \(\mu \geq 5.2\) exactly with pnorm() and from 10,000 draws with rnorm().
Compute the Bayes factor in favor of the point hypothesis \(H_0\!: \mu = 5.2\) with the Savage–Dickey density ratio.
Estimate the same Bayes factor from the 10,000 draws using density(), and compare.
The interval probability in (a) and the Bayes factor in (b) answer different questions. State both questions in words.



Exercise 2.6 (Posterior summaries) Use the \(\text{Beta}(18, 92)\) posterior of the modern art example.

Consider the posterior mean of the log-odds, \(E[\log\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} \mid y]\). Compute it numerically with integrate() and from 10,000 draws with rbeta(). Report the Monte Carlo standard error of the second estimate. An independent check is the identity \(E[\log(\pi/(1-\pi))]=\operatorname{digamma}(a)-\operatorname{digamma}(b)\) for a Beta\((a,b)\) variable, evaluated in R with digamma().
Compute the posterior probability that \(\pi\) lies within \(0.05\) of the board’s target of \(0.2\), both ways.
Compute a 95% HPD interval from the draws with the hpd() function of this chapter and compare it with the central interval. Which is shorter, and by how much?



Exercise 2.7 (The grid, in detail) Use grid_posterior() and log_posterior_logitnormal() from this chapter.

Use midpoint grids pi_grid <- (seq_len(G) - 0.5) / G. Compute the posterior mean and central 95% interval of \(\pi\) under the logit-Normal prior for \(G=10\), \(20\), \(50\), \(200\), and \(1{,}000\). For the grid quantiles, use the first midpoint at which the cumulative probability reaches 0.025 or 0.975. At what \(G\) do the summaries stop changing in the second decimal?
Modify grid_posterior() so that it also returns \(\log f(y)\approx c+\log(\Delta\sum_j w_j)\). Retain the full Binomial probability mass and the normalized prior in log_posterior(). Check against log_ml_H1 for the Beta\((4,6)\) model.
Use the modified function to compute the Bayes factor comparing the \(\text{Beta}(4, 6)\) prior with the logit-Normal prior for the same data. Which prior predicted the data better?




2.9.3 Applied exercises

Exercise 2.8 (Ghosts) The pulse_of_the_nation data in the bayesrules package record, among many other things, whether each of 1,000 survey respondents believes in ghosts (ghosts). Suppose that before seeing the data you place a \(\text{Beta}(2, 3)\) prior on the proportion \(\pi\) of believers, and that a colleague claims that “about a third of people believe in ghosts.”

Load data("pulse_of_the_nation", package = "bayesrules") and tabulate ghosts, including missing values. Identify the recorded categories for yes and no, retain valid yes/no responses, and report the resulting \(y\) and \(n\). Write the posterior for \(\pi\).
Compute the Bayes factor in favor of \(H_0\!: \pi = 1/3\) using the two closed-form marginal likelihoods. Calculate their logarithms with dbinom(..., log = TRUE), lchoose(), and lbeta() before exponentiating their difference.
Compute the same Bayes factor with the Savage–Dickey density ratio and confirm that the two agree.
Repeat (c) with a \(\text{Beta}(1, 1)\) prior and with a \(\text{Beta}(30, 60)\) prior. Interpret the three Bayes factors with the table in this chapter, and explain why they differ.
Explain why a large sample does not by itself guarantee evidence for the point null. How does the observed proportion relative to \(1/3\) affect the comparison? Distinguish evidence favoring a null model from failing to reject a null in a significance test.



Exercise 2.9 (Is the gender effect zero?) Use the two-parameter logistic regression grid and its marginal marginal_beta1. Under \(H_0\), fix \(\beta_1=0\) and retain the \(\text{N}(0,2^2)\) prior on \(\beta_0\). Under \(H_1\), use the independent priors specified in the chapter. This matches the prior on the remaining parameter as required by the Savage–Dickey identity.

The marginal grid probabilities of \(\beta_1\) approximate a density once divided by the grid spacing \(\Delta\). Estimate the marginal posterior density of \(\beta_1\) at \(0\) by linear interpolation of prob / delta between the two grid points closest to 0.
Divide by the prior density dnorm(0, 0, 1) to obtain the Savage–Dickey Bayes factor \(\text{BF}_{01}\) for \(H_0\!: \beta_1 = 0\). Interpret it.
With equal prior probabilities for the two models, what is the posterior probability that the gender effect is zero? Compare it with \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid y)\) from the text and explain why the two numbers answer different questions.
Repeat (a) to (b) with a \(\text{N}(0, 3^2)\) prior on \(\beta_1\), widening the grid as needed. Recompute the grid with sd_beta1 = 3; check both its range and resolution. How does the Bayes factor change? Relate the result to the prior-predictive argument in Exercise 2.4, without assuming that a wider prior must always favor \(H_0\).






Dickey, J. M., & Lientz, B. P. (1970). The weighted likelihood ratio, sharp hypotheses about chances, the order of a Markov chain. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 41(1), 214–226.


Jeffreys, H. (1961). Theory of probability (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.


Johnson, A. A., Ott, M. Q., & Dogucu, M. (2022). Bayes rules! An introduction to applied Bayesian modeling. CRC Press.


Lee, M. D., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2013). Bayesian cognitive modeling: A practical course. Cambridge University Press.


Wagenmakers, E.-J., Lodewyckx, T., Kuriyal, H., & Grasman, R. P. P. P. (2010). Bayesian hypothesis testing for psychologists: A tutorial on the savage–dickey method. Cognitive Psychology, 60(3), 158–189.

title: 3  Markov Chains
text:
3.1 Chains on a finite state space
Suppose you keep a mood diary, recording happy, neutral, or sad each evening. A simple model might allow tomorrow’s mood to depend on today’s. For example, a happy day could be followed by another happy day more often than by a sad one. To use a Markov chain for this model, we make a specific assumption. Once today’s mood is known, knowing earlier moods provides no additional information about tomorrow’s mood. Whether this assumption describes a real diary well is a separate modeling question.
Markov chains also serve a computational purpose. Instead of modeling a person’s mood, we can construct a sequence of parameter values whose long-run behavior represents a posterior distribution. This chapter develops the connection, beginning with a small set of mood states and ending with a chain that samples a grid approximation to a posterior.
We will distinguish the value of a chain at one time from the distribution of that value, and distinguish convergence of distributions from convergence of averages along a chain. These distinctions explain how dependent simulation can support Bayesian inference. Run the following setup before working through the examples.
A state space is the set of values a chain can take. For the mood model it is \(\{\text{happy},\text{neutral},\text{sad}\}\). This is a finite state space because it contains only three possible values. Write \(X^{(t)}\) for the state at time \(t\), with \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\).
The Markov property says that, conditional on the current state, the distribution of the next state does not depend on earlier states: \[
P\!\left(X^{(t+1)}=j\mid X^{(t)}=i,X^{(t-1)},\ldots,X^{(0)}\right)
=P\!\left(X^{(t+1)}=j\mid X^{(t)}=i\right).
\] Here \(i\) is the current state and \(j\) is the next state. We consider time-homogeneous chains, whose transition probabilities do not change with \(t\), and write these probabilities as \(P_{ij}\). Numbering happy, neutral, and sad as states 1, 2, and 3 gives, for example, \[
P_{12}=P(\text{neutral tomorrow}\mid\text{happy today}).
\]
Arrange the transition probabilities with one row for each current state and one column for each next state. The following matrix defines our illustrative mood model. In R, byrow = TRUE fills the entries row by row, and dimnames attaches the mood labels to both rows and columns:
moods <- c("happy", "neutral", "sad")
P <- matrix(c(0.70, 0.25, 0.05,
              0.20, 0.50, 0.30,
              0.20, 0.40, 0.40),
            nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(moods, moods))
P
#>         happy neutral  sad
#> happy     0.7    0.25 0.05
#> neutral   0.2    0.50 0.30
#> sad       0.2    0.40 0.40
Read it by rows. After a happy day, the next day is happy with probability \(0.70\), neutral with probability \(0.25\), and sad with probability \(0.05\). After a sad day, the mood stays sad with probability \(0.40\), recovers to neutral with probability \(0.40\), and jumps straight to happy with probability \(0.20\). Every row is a probability distribution over tomorrow, so every row sums to one:
rowSums(P)
#>   happy neutral     sad 
#>       1       1       1
The column sums need not equal one. A matrix with non-negative entries and row sums of one is called a stochastic matrix. Together with an initial distribution, it specifies a time-homogeneous Markov chain.
A note on notation. In this chapter the states are moods, so we call the chain \(X^{(t)}\) and the states \(i\) and \(j\). From Section 3.6 onward, the states are candidate values of a parameter, and we write the chain as \(\theta^{(t)}\), as in Appendix B. The states then describe a computational sequence rather than an observed sequence of moods. We use bold \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) for a vector of stationary probabilities and plain \(\pi\) for an unknown proportion.

title: 3  Markov Chains
text:
Specifying a finite-state Markov chain

Specify the possible states, an initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}\) over them, and a transition matrix \(\mathbf P\). Entry \(P_{ij}\) is the probability of moving from state \(i\) to state \(j\) in one step.
A fixed initial state is a special case. Starting happy with certainty gives \(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}=(1,0,0)\). Alternatively, we can draw the initial state using any specified probability vector over the three moods.








3.1.1 Simulating the chain
At each transition, select the row for the current mood and draw the next mood using that row’s probabilities. sample() takes the state labels, the number of draws, and the probabilities. For example, sample(moods, 1, prob = P["happy", ]) generates a possible next state after a happy day.
A simulated chain of length \(N\) contains the states \(X^{(0)},\ldots,X^{(N-1)}\), including the initial state. The function below makes n_iter transitions and returns one state more than that, because the initial state is included. With n_iter = 60, it returns 61 states at times 0 through 60. The first stored element, x[1], represents \(X^{(0)}\).

simulate_chain <- function(P, init, n_iter) {
  states <- rownames(P)
  x <- character(n_iter + 1)
  x[1] <- init
  for (t in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    x[t + 1] <- sample(states, size = 1, prob = P[x[t], ])
  }
  x
}


set.seed(84735)
diary <- simulate_chain(P, init = "happy", n_iter = 60)
head(diary, 14)
#>  [1] "happy"   "neutral" "sad"     "sad"     "happy"   "neutral" "neutral"
#>  [8] "sad"     "sad"     "sad"     "neutral" "happy"   "happy"   "happy"

Consecutive entries can repeat. For example, the probability of remaining happy for one more day is \(P_{11}=0.70\). Figure 3.1 shows the resulting path. Each point is one realized state, not a probability distribution.

tibble(day = 0:60, mood = factor(diary, levels = rev(moods))) |>
  ggplot(aes(day, mood, group = 1)) +
  geom_step(color = "#552E6B") +
  geom_point(color = "#552E6B", size = 1) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = NULL)







Figure 3.1: A mood diary simulated for 60 transitions, with its happy initial state shown at day zero. Consecutive states can be identical. The path records one sequence of outcomes.







3.1.2 Where will the chain be in \(t\) days?
The transition matrix answers questions about tomorrow. To ask about the day after tomorrow, we sum over what can happen in between. Starting from state \(i\), the chain reaches state \(j\) in two steps by passing through some state \(k\) on day one, so \[
P\!\left(X^{(t+2)} = j \mid X^{(t)} = i\right) = \sum_{k} P_{ik} P_{kj},
\] The index \(k\) runs over the possible intermediate states. Each product describes a two-step route, and summing the products accounts for all those routes. This is the \((i,j)\) entry of \(\mathbf P^2\). More generally, entry \((i,j)\) of \(\mathbf P^t\) is the probability of reaching \(j\) after \(t\) transitions from \(i\).
In R, %*% performs matrix multiplication, whereas P^2 squares each entry separately. The function below begins with the identity matrix, representing zero transitions, and multiplies by P once per transition. With t = 0, seq_len(t) is empty and the identity is returned.

mat_power <- function(P, t) {
  out <- diag(nrow(P))
  dimnames(out) <- dimnames(P)
  for (k in seq_len(t)) out <- out %*% P
  out
}
mat_power(P, 2)
#>         happy neutral  sad
#> happy    0.55    0.32 0.13
#> neutral  0.30    0.42 0.28
#> sad      0.30    0.41 0.29



Quiz yourself!

Today is a happy day. Compute by hand, from \(\mathbf{P}\), the probability that the day after tomorrow is sad. Check your answer against mat_power(P, 2).

The distribution at a given time is a different object from one realized state. The vector \[
\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}=
\big(P(X^{(t)}=\text{happy}),P(X^{(t)}=\text{neutral}),P(X^{(t)}=\text{sad})\big)
\] lists the probabilities of the three possible moods at time \(t\). Its entries sum to one. Starting happy with certainty gives \(\boldsymbol\mu^{(0)}=(1,0,0)\); one transition gives \((0.70,0.25,0.05)\).
For a less certain start, suppose \(\boldsymbol\mu^{(0)}=(0.2,0.5,0.3)\). The probability of a happy day after one transition is \[
0.2\times0.70+0.5\times0.20+0.3\times0.20=0.30.
\] The other entries are calculated in the same way. Matrix multiplication performs all three weighted sums:

mu0 <- c(happy = 0.2, neutral = 0.5, sad = 0.3)
mu0 %*% P
#>      happy neutral  sad
#> [1,]   0.3    0.42 0.28

The result is \((0.30,0.42,0.28)\). It describes probabilities across possible realizations of the chain, not three moods experienced simultaneously by one person. We use row vectors, so the update is \[
\boldsymbol\mu^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}\mathbf P,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}=\boldsymbol\mu^{(0)}\mathbf P^t.
\tag{3.1}\]
Each row of \(\mathbf P^t\) corresponds to a different fixed starting state. Compare the rows after five and twenty transitions:

round(mat_power(P, 5), 4)
#>          happy neutral    sad
#> happy   0.4187  0.3707 0.2105
#> neutral 0.3875  0.3825 0.2300
#> sad     0.3875  0.3825 0.2300
round(mat_power(P, 20), 4)
#>         happy neutral    sad
#> happy     0.4  0.3778 0.2222
#> neutral   0.4  0.3778 0.2222
#> sad       0.4  0.3778 0.2222

After twenty transitions, the rows agree to four decimal places. The probability of a happy state is approximately 0.4 for any of the three starts. This is approximate agreement of state distributions; the individual paths still fluctuate.

title: 3  Markov Chains
text:
3.2 Stationary distributions


Stationary distribution

A probability vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_S)\) over the \(S\) states is a stationary distribution of the chain with transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) if \[
\boldsymbol{\pi} \mathbf{P} = \boldsymbol{\pi}, \qquad \text{that is,} \qquad \sum_{i} \pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j \quad \text{for every state } j.
\] If \(X^{(t)}\) is distributed according to \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), then so is \(X^{(t+1)}\), and so is every later state.

The definition says that \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is a fixed point of the update \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \mapsto \boldsymbol{\mu} \mathbf{P}\). If you start the chain by drawing \(X^{(0)}\) from \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), the distribution of the state never changes, even though the state itself keeps moving. For a population of diary keepers following this model, the expected proportions in the three moods would then remain constant. Realized proportions in a finite population can still fluctuate. The word stationary describes the distribution, not an unchanging individual mood. We first solve its defining equations, then compare matrix powers and simulated frequencies.
Solve the equation. Write \(h\), \(u\), and \(s\) for the stationary probabilities of happy, neutral, and sad. The first stationary equation and \(h+u+s=1\) give \[
h=0.70h+0.20u+0.20s=0.70h+0.20(1-h),
\qquad 0.50h=0.20,
\] so \(h=0.40\). The neutral equation is \[
u=0.25(0.40)+0.50u+0.40(0.60-u)
=0.34+0.10u.
\] Thus \(u=0.34/0.90=17/45\), and \(s=0.60-17/45=2/9\). The stationary vector is \((0.40,17/45,2/9)\).
For a larger matrix, eigenvectors provide a numerical way to solve the same equation. The condition \(\boldsymbol{\pi} \mathbf{P} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\) says that \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is a left eigenvector of \(\mathbf{P}\) with eigenvalue 1. Equivalently, transposing both sides, \(\boldsymbol{\pi}^\top\) is an ordinary (right) eigenvector of \(\mathbf{P}^\top\), which is what eigen() computes. If you have encountered principal component analysis (PCA), the operation may be familiar. PCA finds eigenvectors of a covariance matrix to identify directions of variation. Here the matrix is \(\mathbf P^\top\), and an eigenvalue of one identifies a vector unchanged by the probability update. We rescale that eigenvector so its entries sum to one; no knowledge of PCA is needed for this calculation.
The function below is used for chains with a unique stationary distribution. If there are several stationary distributions, the eigenvalue-one condition alone does not select a particular mixture.

stationary <- function(P) {
  e <- eigen(t(P))
  k <- which.min(abs(e$values - 1))     # the eigenvalue equal to 1
  v <- Re(e$vectors[, k])
  setNames(v / sum(v), rownames(P))
}
pi_mood <- stationary(P)
pi_mood
#>     happy   neutral       sad 
#> 0.4000000 0.3777778 0.2222222

For this chain, long-run frequencies approach about 40% of days are happy, 38% neutral, and 22% sad. We can check the defining equation directly:

pi_mood %*% P
#>      happy   neutral       sad
#> [1,]   0.4 0.3777778 0.2222222

Raise \(\mathbf{P}\) to a large power. For this chain, each row approaches the stationary vector as the power increases. The rows agree approximately, rather than becoming exactly equal after a finite number of transitions. The conditions supporting this approximation are stated in the next section.

mat_power(P, 50)[1, ]
#>     happy   neutral       sad 
#> 0.4000000 0.3777778 0.2222222

Run the chain and count. The third way is the one that matters for the rest of the book. Simulate a long diary, and count how often each mood occurs:

set.seed(84735)
long_diary <- simulate_chain(P, init = "sad", n_iter = 20000)
freq_mood <- table(factor(long_diary[-1], levels = moods)) / (length(long_diary) - 1)
freq_mood
#> 
#>   happy neutral     sad 
#> 0.39535 0.37980 0.22485

The simulated frequencies approximate \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) (Figure 3.2). We omit the initial state when counting the 20,000 generated states. Unlike the eigenvector and matrix-power calculations, these estimates vary from simulation to simulation. The ergodic theorem below explains why averaging along an appropriate chain can estimate properties of its stationary distribution.

tibble(mood = factor(rep(moods, 3), levels = moods),
       method = rep(c("Eigenvector", "Matrix power", "Simulated frequencies"), each = 3),
       probability = c(pi_mood, mat_power(P, 50)[1, ], as.numeric(freq_mood))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mood, probability, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#552E6B", "#9E7BB5", "#ECECEC"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Probability")







Figure 3.2: Stationary probabilities from an eigenvector calculation and a large matrix power, compared with frequency estimates from 20,000 generated states. The simulated frequencies have Monte Carlo error.





How quickly does the starting distribution matter less? Figure 3.3 follows all three mood probabilities from each possible initial state, using Equation 3.1. These are calculated probabilities, not three simulated diary paths.

forgetting <- expand_grid(start = moods, day = 0:12) |>
  mutate(distribution = map2(start, day, \(s, t) {
    mu0 <- setNames(as.numeric(moods == s), moods)
    drop(mu0 %*% mat_power(P, t))
  })) |>
  unnest_wider(distribution) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(moods), names_to = "mood", values_to = "probability") |>
  mutate(mood = factor(mood, levels = moods, labels = c("Happy", "Neutral", "Sad")))
stationary_lines <- tibble(mood = factor(c("Happy", "Neutral", "Sad"),
                                        levels = c("Happy", "Neutral", "Sad")),
                           probability = as.numeric(pi_mood))
ggplot(forgetting, aes(day, probability, color = start, linetype = start)) +
  geom_hline(data = stationary_lines, aes(yintercept = probability),
             linetype = "dotted", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ mood) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("happy" = "#552E6B", "neutral" = "#9E7BB5", "sad" = "gray50"), name = "Initial mood") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("happy" = "solid", "neutral" = "dashed", "sad" = "dotdash"), name = "Initial mood") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  labs(x = "Day t", y = "State probability")







Figure 3.3: State probabilities from each of the three fixed initial moods. Thin black dotted lines mark the stationary probabilities. In the Happy panel, the neutral and sad starts produce exactly the same curve, so only two distinct colored curves are visible. The other panels show how these starts differ for the remaining moods.





The overlapping curves in the Happy panel have a numerical explanation. A neutral or sad day is followed by a happy day with the same probability, 0.20. If \(p_t=P(X^{(t)}=\text{happy})\), then \[
p_{t+1}=0.70p_t+0.20(1-p_t)=0.20+0.50p_t.
\] Neutral and sad starts both have \(p_0=0\), so their happy-state probabilities agree at every time. Subtract the stationary happy probability, 0.40, from the update: \[
p_{t+1}-0.40=0.50(p_t-0.40),
\qquad
p_t=0.40+0.50^t(p_0-0.40).
\] For a happy start, the sequence begins \(1,0.70,0.55,0.475\). The difference from 0.40 halves at each transition. This explains the rate in this particular panel.
Eigenvalues connect this repeated multiplication to the matrix calculation. The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf P\) are 1, 0.5, and 0.1. The eigenvalue 1 corresponds to the stationary vector. In this example, the other components shrink at rates \(0.5^t\) and \(0.1^t\). A component multiplied by 0.99 at each transition would decline much more slowly; after 100 transitions it would retain about 37% of its initial size, because \(0.99^{100}\approx0.37\). Eigenvalues near one in absolute value can therefore indicate slow decay of initial differences.
Discarding initial states is one way to reduce the effect of an arbitrary start when estimating posterior summaries. It does not make later states independent. In Chapter 4, warm-up also includes the adaptation of sampler settings.

title: 3  Markov Chains
text:
3.3 Irreducibility, aperiodicity, and convergence
The mood chain has a unique stationary distribution, and its state distribution approaches that distribution from every start. Every finite-state chain has at least one stationary distribution, but uniqueness and convergence require further conditions. The following examples separate those questions.
A chain with two closed groups of states. Consider a model with two types of diary keepers. Type A can be happy or neutral; type B can be sad or gloomy. In this model a person’s type stays fixed. Combining the four moods into one transition matrix gives two groups between which an individual chain cannot move:

P_split <- matrix(c(0.7, 0.3, 0.0, 0.0,
                    0.4, 0.6, 0.0, 0.0,
                    0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.5,
                    0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 0.8),
                  nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("happy", "neutral", "sad", "gloomy"),
                                  c("happy", "neutral", "sad", "gloomy")))
mat_power(P_split, 50)
#>             happy   neutral       sad    gloomy
#> happy   0.5714286 0.4285714 0.0000000 0.0000000
#> neutral 0.5714286 0.4285714 0.0000000 0.0000000
#> sad     0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2857143 0.7142857
#> gloomy  0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2857143 0.7142857

Rows for type A approach \((4/7,3/7,0,0)\), while rows for type B approach \((0,0,2/7,5/7)\). Each vector is stationary, and any weighted average of the two is stationary as well. Starting in one group does not tell us the distribution of states in the other group.
This chain is reducible. A chain is irreducible if every state can be reached from every other in some finite number of transitions with positive probability. The mood chain with three states is irreducible, because every entry of its matrix is positive.
A chain that never settles. Now suppose a diary keeper’s moods alternate: a happy day is always followed by a sad one, and a sad day by a happy one.

P_swing <- matrix(c(0, 1,
                    1, 0),
                  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("happy", "sad"), c("happy", "sad")))
mat_power(P_swing, 7)
#>       happy sad
#> happy     0   1
#> sad       1   0
mat_power(P_swing, 8)
#>       happy sad
#> happy     1   0
#> sad       0   1

This chain is irreducible and has the unique stationary distribution \((0.5,0.5)\). Check it by multiplication: \[
(0.5,0.5)\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=(0.5,0.5).
\] The stationary equation can hold even when the distribution from a fixed starting state oscillates. But \(\mathbf{P}^t\) never converges: it is \(\mathbf{P}\) for odd \(t\) and the identity for even \(t\). Started on a happy day, the chain is happy on every even day with certainty, forever (Figure 3.4). From that fixed initial state, the distribution of \(X^{(t)}\) does not approach \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\). Starting with \(\boldsymbol\pi=(0.5,0.5)\) would be different: That distribution is already stationary.
This chain is periodic with period 2: it can only return to a state after an even number of steps.
The period of a state is the greatest common divisor of its possible positive return times: The largest integer dividing every such time. Return times 2, 4, 6, and so on have common divisor 2. If returns are possible in both 2 and 3 transitions, their greatest common divisor is 1. A chain is aperiodic when every state has period 1.
A useful sufficient condition in an irreducible chain is a self-loop. If some \(P_{ii} > 0\), the chain can return to \(i\) in one step, so the period of \(i\) is 1, and in an irreducible chain all states share the same period. The mood chain has positive entries on its diagonal, so it is aperiodic.

p_happy <- function(P, start, t) {
  mu0 <- setNames(as.numeric(rownames(P) == start), rownames(P))
  (mu0 %*% mat_power(P, t))[1, "happy"]
}
bind_rows(
  tibble(chain = "Mood chain", day = 0:12,
         p = map_dbl(day, \(t) p_happy(P, "happy", t)), pi = pi_mood["happy"]),
  tibble(chain = "Alternating chain", day = 0:12,
         p = map_dbl(day, \(t) p_happy(P_swing, "happy", t)), pi = 0.5)
) |>
  mutate(chain = factor(chain, levels = c("Mood chain", "Alternating chain"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(day, p)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = pi), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = "#552E6B") + geom_point(color = "#552E6B") +
  facet_wrap(~ chain) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 12, by = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Day t", y = expression(P(X^(t) == "happy")))







Figure 3.4: \(P(X^{(t)} = \text{happy})\) for a chain started on a happy day: the mood chain (left) converges to \(\pi_{\text{happy}}\), the alternating chain (right) swings between 1 and 0 forever, even though \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = (0.5, 0.5)\) is its stationary distribution.







The convergence theorem

Let \(\mathbf{P}\) be the transition matrix of a Markov chain on a finite state space.

If the chain is irreducible, it has exactly one stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), and every state has \(\pi_i > 0\).
If the chain is also aperiodic, then \(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)} \mathbf{P}^t \to \boldsymbol{\pi}\) as \(t \to \infty\) for every starting distribution \(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(0)}\). Equivalently, every row of \(\mathbf{P}^t\) converges to \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\).


These finite-state results are developed in Norris (1997) and Robert & Casella (2004, Chapter 6). The examples illustrate why both conditions matter. The split chain has more than one stationary distribution; the alternating chain has one, but does not converge to it from a fixed state. In the sampling construction later in this chapter, we check stationarity, irreducibility, and aperiodicity separately.


Quiz yourself!

A chain on three states has transition matrix \[
\mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
\] Is it irreducible? What are the possible return times, and is it aperiodic? Check whether \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\) is stationary by multiplying it by \(\mathbf P\). Starting from \(\boldsymbol\mu^{(0)}=(1,0,0)\), does the state distribution converge to that vector? Use the theorem to explain your conclusions.

title: 3  Markov Chains
text:
3.4 The ergodic theorem
Convergence of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}\) to \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is a statement about the distribution of the state on a single day \(t\). For Monte Carlo estimation, we usually average over many states from one chain, as in the calculation of freq_mood. The ergodic theorem establishes the convergence of these time averages. It is the Markov chain version of the law of large numbers from Chapter 1.


The ergodic theorem (informal)

Let \(X^{(0)}, X^{(1)}, \ldots\) be an irreducible Markov chain on a finite state space with stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), and let \(h\) be any function of the state. Then, whatever the starting state, \[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} h\!\left(X^{(t)}\right) \;\longrightarrow\; \sum_{i} h(i)\, \pi_i \qquad \text{as } N \to \infty.
\] \(N\) is the number of sampled states included in the average. Long-run averages along one chain converge to expectations under the stationary distribution.

Take \(h(i) = 1\) if \(i\) is happy and \(0\) otherwise. The theorem says that the fraction of happy days in a long diary converges to \(\pi_{\text{happy}}\), which is what Figure 3.2 showed. Figure 3.5 shows the convergence in progress: three diaries of 2,000 transitions, started in the three moods, and for each the running fraction of happy days over the 2,001 days including day zero. Here the running fractions include the initial state, so they begin at 1, 0, and 0. Including one initial value does not change their limiting values, although finite-simulation estimates differ.

set.seed(84735)
running <- map(moods, \(s) {
  x <- simulate_chain(P, init = s, n_iter = 2000)
  tibble(start = s, day = 0:2000, running_mean = cummean(x == "happy"))
}) |> list_rbind()

ggplot(running, aes(day, running_mean, color = start)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pi_mood["happy"], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#552E6B", "#9E7BB5", "gray50"), name = "Started") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "Fraction of happy days")







Figure 3.5: Running fraction of happy days in three simulated diaries of 2,000 transitions, one started in each mood. The dashed line is \(\pi_{\text{happy}}\). The finite-run estimates fluctuate; the finite-state ergodic theorem establishes their common limiting value.





The alternating chain illustrates the difference between the two kinds of convergence. Starting happy, its state distribution alternates forever between \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\). Its time average of the happy-state indicator nevertheless approaches 0.5. Aperiodicity is needed for the finite-state distribution-convergence result, but not for this finite-state ergodic theorem.
Dependence also does not invalidate the time-average result. It does affect numerical precision. To isolate that effect, compare 365 observations from the mood chain with 365 independent draws from its stationary distribution. We draw the chain’s initial state from \(\boldsymbol\pi\) so that all 365 states have that marginal distribution and the comparison is not confounded by a fixed starting mood.

set.seed(84735)
one_year <- function() {
  initial_mood <- sample(moods, size = 1, prob = pi_mood)
  chain <- simulate_chain(P, init = initial_mood, n_iter = 364)
  iid   <- sample(moods, size = 365, replace = TRUE, prob = pi_mood)
  c(chain = mean(chain == "happy"), iid = mean(iid == "happy"))
}
years <- map(1:500, \(i) one_year()) |> bind_rows()
years |> summarize(across(everything(), list(mean = mean, sd = sd)))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   chain_mean chain_sd iid_mean iid_sd
#>        <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1      0.401   0.0422    0.401 0.0247

Both estimates have expectation \(\pi_{\text{happy}}\). In this experiment, the standard deviation across the dependent-chain estimates is about 1.7 times the standard deviation across the independent estimates. The persistence of moods makes the chain estimates more variable. The ergodic theorem establishes their limiting behavior, but does not supply a standard error for a finite run. Chapter 4 develops effective sample size and Monte Carlo standard errors for dependent draws.

title: 3  Markov Chains
text:
3.5 Detailed balance
So far, we have specified a transition matrix and investigated its stationary distribution. For posterior simulation, we work in the other direction. We specify the target distribution and choose transitions that preserve it. Many different transition matrices can have the same stationary distribution. Detailed balance provides a convenient way to construct one of them.
Suppose the current state has distribution \(\boldsymbol\pi\). The product \(\pi_iP_{ij}\) is the joint probability of being in \(i\) now and in \(j\) next. It can also be interpreted as an expected fraction of transitions in a large population of diary keepers. We call it the probability flow from \(i\) to \(j\) (Hanada & Matsuura, 2022, Section 3.4). Stationarity says that the total flow into each state equals the total flow out of it, so that no state gains or loses probability: \[
\underbrace{\sum_{i} \pi_i P_{ij}}_{\text{flow into } j} = \pi_j = \underbrace{\sum_{k} \pi_j P_{jk}}_{\text{flow out of } j}.
\] This is a balance condition: it constrains the sums. Detailed balance asks for more, namely that the flow between each pair of states is the same in both directions.


Detailed balance

A transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) satisfies detailed balance with respect to a probability vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) if \[
\pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j P_{ji} \qquad \text{for all states } i, j.
\tag{3.2}\] If detailed balance holds, then \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is a stationary distribution of the chain.

To show why detailed balance implies stationarity, fix any next state \(j\) and sum over the current states \(i\): \[
\sum_{i} \pi_i P_{ij} = \sum_{i} \pi_j P_{ji} = \pi_j \sum_{i} P_{ji} = \pi_j.
\] The first equality is detailed balance, applied to every term. The second pulls \(\pi_j\) out of the sum, because it does not depend on \(i\). The third uses that row \(j\) of \(\mathbf{P}\) sums to one. The left-hand side is the \(j\)th entry of \(\boldsymbol{\pi} \mathbf{P}\), so we have shown \(\boldsymbol{\pi} \mathbf{P} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\). Thus pairwise balance ensures that the total probability arriving in each state equals its stationary probability. The proof uses the row-sum condition as well as detailed balance.
Detailed balance is sufficient for stationarity, not necessary. The mood chain is an example. Its stationary distribution certainly balances, but look at the flows in each direction:

flow <- P
for (i in seq_len(nrow(P))) {
  flow[i, ] <- pi_mood[i] * P[i, ]
}
round(flow, 3)
#>         happy neutral   sad
#> happy   0.280   0.100 0.020
#> neutral 0.076   0.189 0.113
#> sad     0.044   0.089 0.089
round(flow - t(flow), 3)       # zero everywhere if detailed balance holds
#>          happy neutral    sad
#> happy    0.000   0.024 -0.024
#> neutral -0.024   0.000  0.024
#> sad      0.024  -0.024  0.000

The loop multiplies every entry in row \(i\) by \(\pi_i\). For example, the happy-to-neutral flow is \(0.40\times0.25=0.10\), whereas the neutral-to-happy flow is \((17/45)\times0.20\approx0.0756\). Transposing the matrix reverses each pair of states, so flow - t(flow) compares the two directions.


Quiz yourself!

What does a positive entry in flow - t(flow) mean? Why are its diagonal entries zero even when detailed balance fails? Would zero column sums of this difference be enough to establish detailed balance?

More diary keepers go from happy to neutral each day than from neutral to happy, more go from neutral to sad than back, and more go from sad to happy than the other way. The flows do not match pairwise; instead there is a steady circulation happy \(\to\) neutral \(\to\) sad \(\to\) happy, of about 0.024 of the population per day, and every state still receives as much as it gives. A chain satisfying detailed balance is reversible when started in its stationary distribution. Reversing the order of a stationary sequence does not change its joint probability law. The mood model has a stationary distribution but does not satisfy detailed balance, so reversibility is not required for stationarity.

3.5.1 What detailed balance guarantees
Detailed balance implies that the specified target distribution is stationary. It does not imply irreducibility or aperiodicity.

The identity matrix leaves every state where it is. It satisfies detailed balance for any target vector, because all flows between different states are zero. Yet it is reducible and cannot explore the target.
The alternating two-state chain satisfies detailed balance for \((0.5,0.5)\), because the flow in either direction is 0.5. It is irreducible but periodic.

For a finite-state sampler, the checks therefore serve different purposes:







Check
What it establishes




Detailed balance with the target
The target is stationary


Irreducibility
There is a unique stationary distribution; time averages converge to its expectations


Irreducibility and aperiodicity
State distributions approach the stationary distribution from any start





3.5.2 Choosing transitions for a target
Consider a target with two states and probabilities \(\boldsymbol\pi=(0.25,0.75)\). We can choose \(P_{12}=0.30\) and determine the reverse probability from detailed balance: \[
0.25\times0.30=0.75\times P_{21},\qquad P_{21}=0.10.
\] Complete each row by assigning its remaining probability to staying in the same state: \[
\mathbf P_* =\begin{pmatrix}0.70&0.30\\0.10&0.90\end{pmatrix}.
\] Both cross-state flows are 0.075. Direct multiplication confirms that \((0.25,0.75)\mathbf P_*=(0.25,0.75)\). The chain is also irreducible, because both cross-state transitions have positive probability, and aperiodic, because it can stay in a state.
The choice is not unique. Smaller cross-state transition probabilities can satisfy the same equation but produce a slower-moving chain. In general, for positive target probabilities and a pair of permitted moves, detailed balance can be written \[
\frac{P_{ij}}{P_{ji}}=\frac{\pi_j}{\pi_i}.
\] If the target is known up to a common normalizing constant, that constant cancels in the ratio on the right. We can therefore design transitions using relative target weights. The grid construction below applies this idea to a posterior.


Quiz yourself!

A chain has only two states, with \(P_{12} = a\) and \(P_{21} = b\), both positive. Find its stationary distribution, and show that every such two-state chain satisfies detailed balance. Why is the three-state mood chain different?

title: 3  Markov Chains
section: 3.6 From transition matrices to transition kernels
text:
3.6 From transition matrices to transition kernels
Most parameters in this book take values in intervals or in a continuous space with several coordinates. We can no longer list a transition probability for each possible next value in a finite matrix. Instead, a transition kernel specifies the distribution of the next state given the current state.

3.6.1 A Normal transition example
Suppose the transition rule is \[
\theta^{(t+1)}=0.6\theta^{(t)}+0.8Z^{(t+1)},
\qquad Z^{(t+1)}\sim\text{N}(0,1),
\] where each new \(Z^{(t+1)}\) is independent of the earlier states and random draws. Given a current value \(\theta\), the next state has a Normal distribution with mean \(0.6\theta\) and standard deviation \(0.8\): \[
\theta^{(t+1)}\mid\theta^{(t)}=\theta
\sim\text{N}(0.6\theta,0.8^2).
\] For example, from \(\theta=1\), the next-state distribution is \(\text{N}(0.6,0.8^2)\). We can generate possible next values or calculate an interval probability:

set.seed(84735)
current <- 1
rnorm(5, mean = 0.6 * current, sd = 0.8)
#> [1] 1.1337862 0.5009278 1.2246941 0.7895346 1.2372088
pnorm(1, mean = 0.6 * current, sd = 0.8) -
  pnorm(0, mean = 0.6 * current, sd = 0.8)
#> [1] 0.4648351

The five draws are independent possible next states from the same current value; they are not five consecutive states of a chain. The last calculation gives a probability of about 0.465 that the next state lies between zero and one. To generate a chain, use each new state as the current value for the next transition.

kernel_curves <- crossing(current = c(-1, 0, 1), next_value = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 501)) |>
  mutate(density = dnorm(next_value, mean = 0.6 * current, sd = 0.8),
         current = factor(current))
ggplot(kernel_curves, aes(next_value, density, color = current, linetype = current)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#9E7BB5", "#552E6B", "gray40"), name = "Current state") +
  labs(x = "Next state", y = "Conditional density", linetype = "Current state")







Figure 3.6: Conditional densities for the Normal transition rule, from current states -1, 0, and 1. Each curve integrates to one and describes a possible next value. Changing the current state shifts the mean to 0.6 times that state. These conditional densities are different from a stationary density.







A useful property of Normal variables

If \(X\) and \(Z\) are independent Normal variables, then \(aX+bZ\) is also Normal. Its mean and variance are \[
\mathbb E[aX+bZ]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Z],
\] \[
\operatorname{Var}(aX+bZ)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^2\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\] Independence is essential here: without it, the variance also includes a covariance term.

To check whether the standard Normal distribution is stationary, suppose the current state has distribution \(\theta^{(t)}\sim\text{N}(0,1)\). The new draw \(Z^{(t+1)}\sim\text{N}(0,1)\) is independent of that state. By the property above, the next state, \[
\theta^{(t+1)}=0.6\theta^{(t)}+0.8Z^{(t+1)},
\] is also Normal. Its mean is zero, and its variance is \[
0.6^2\times1+0.8^2\times1=0.36+0.64=1.
\] Thus \(\theta^{(t+1)}\sim\text{N}(0,1)\): one transition preserves the standard Normal distribution, establishing stationarity. The individual values still change; it is their distribution that stays the same.


3.6.2 When a transition has a density
When the next-state distribution has a density, write it as \(K(\theta,\theta')\), with \(\theta\) the current state and \(\theta'\) the next state. Fixing \(\theta\) gives the continuous counterpart of one row of a transition matrix. For the Normal example, \[
K(\theta,\theta')=\frac{1}{0.8\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\theta'-0.6\theta)^2}{2(0.8)^2}\right].
\] A density value is not a transition probability. The probability of reaching an interval is an area: \[
P(a<\theta^{(t+1)}<b\mid\theta^{(t)}=\theta)
=\int_a^b K(\theta,\theta')\,d\theta'.
\] For kernels that have such a density, the finite-state equations take the following forms:







Finite states
Transitions with a density




\(P_{ij}\) is a probability of the next state
\(K(\theta,\theta')\) is a density for the next state


\(\sum_jP_{ij}=1\)
\(\int K(\theta,\theta')\,d\theta'=1\)


\(\sum_i\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_j\)
\(\int f(\theta)K(\theta,\theta')\,d\theta=f(\theta')\)


\(\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}\)
\(f(\theta)K(\theta,\theta')=f(\theta')K(\theta',\theta)\)



Here \(f\) is the candidate stationary density. Detailed balance implies stationarity by integration, just as it did by summation: \[
\begin{aligned}
\int f(\theta)K(\theta,\theta')\,d\theta
&=\int f(\theta')K(\theta',\theta)\,d\theta\\
&=f(\theta')\int K(\theta',\theta)\,d\theta
=f(\theta').
\end{aligned}
\] The final integral is one because, with \(\theta'\) fixed, \(K(\theta',\theta)\) integrates over all possible next states \(\theta\).

title: 3  Markov Chains
text:
3.7 A first hand-built chain
We now use a Markov chain as a computational tool. Its states will be candidate parameter values, rather than observed moods. We use detailed balance to preserve a target posterior approximation, then check irreducibility and aperiodicity. Keeping the state space finite lets us verify the complete transition matrix.
Consider a survey asking what proportion \(\pi\) of students had a sad day yesterday. You ask \(n=100\) students and 14 say yes, so \(Y \mid \pi \sim \text{Bin}(100, \pi)\) with \(Y = 14\). For a prior, suppose you expected sad days to be fairly common, say around 40% but with real uncertainty, and chose \(\pi \sim \text{Beta}(4, 6)\). The Beta-Binomial model then gives the posterior \(\pi \mid Y = 14 \sim \text{Beta}(18, 92)\). The known Beta posterior provides a benchmark for the numerical calculation. This survey model is separate from the transition model for an individual’s daily moods.
Use \(G=100\) grid midpoints between zero and one, as in Chapter 2. Evaluate the unnormalized posterior on the log scale. For plotting and matrix checks, also form relative weights by subtracting their maximum before exponentiating:

G <- 100
grid <- (seq_len(G) - 0.5) / G
log_target <- dbeta(grid, 4, 6, log = TRUE) +
  dbinom(14, size = 100, prob = grid, log = TRUE)
target <- exp(log_target - max(log_target))
