The first iteration is the move illustrated in Figure 7.3. The target density is lower at the proposed state, and the Metropolis rule would accept the move with probability \(0.6\). But the log-Normal proposal favors this downward move over its reverse by a factor of two, and the Hastings correction reduces the acceptance ratio to \(0.3\). The uniform draw of \(0.45\) would have accepted the move under the Metropolis rule, but exceeds the corrected ratio, so the move is rejected.
In the second iteration, the proposal lands near the posterior mode. The target ratio is \(8.9\), far larger than the correction of \(0.65\) can offset. The acceptance ratio therefore exceeds one, and the move is accepted without a uniform draw.
In the third iteration, the proposed value is larger, but its target density is lower. The target ratio is \(0.83\), and the Hastings correction of \(1.2\) increases the acceptance ratio to \(0.99\). The uniform draw of \(0.9\) would have rejected the move under the Metropolis rule, but falls below the corrected ratio, so the move is accepted. The recorded states are \((1, 0.65, 0.78)\).


Quiz yourself!

A chain is at \(\sigma^{(t)} = 2\) and the log-Normal proposal produces \(\sigma^\star = 4\). The unnormalized target is \(f(2) = 0.40\) and \(f(4) = 0.10\). What is the acceptance probability under the Metropolis rule that ignores the asymmetry, and what is it under Metropolis–Hastings?



7.1.4 A general Metropolis–Hastings sampler in R
The sampler needs two functions that metropolis() did not need. The first, propose(current), generates a candidate value given the current state. The second, log_q(to, from), evaluates the log proposal density \(\log q(\texttt{to} \mid \texttt{from})\). We pass both as arguments. Everything else follows metropolis() from Chapter 5, with one additional term in the log acceptance ratio, the log Hastings correction.

metropolis_hastings <- function(log_target, init, n_iter, propose, log_q, ...) {
  d <- length(init)
  draws <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_iter, ncol = d)
  current <- init
  current_lp <- log_target(current, ...)
  n_accept <- 0

  for (t in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    proposal <- propose(current)                             # 1. propose
    proposal_lp <- log_target(proposal, ...)
    log_r <- (proposal_lp - current_lp) +                    # 2. compare ...
      (log_q(current, proposal) - log_q(proposal, current))  # ... with the Hastings correction
    if (log(runif(1)) < log_r) {                             # 3. accept ...
      current <- proposal
      current_lp <- proposal_lp
      n_accept <- n_accept + 1
    }
    draws[t, ] <- current                                    # ... or stay and record
  }

  colnames(draws) <- if (d == 1) "theta" else paste0("theta_", seq_len(d))
  list(
    draws = as_tibble(draws) |> mutate(iteration = seq_len(n_iter), .before = 1),
    accept_rate = n_accept / n_iter
  )
}

For the log-Normal proposal with \(c = 0.5\), the two helper functions are one line each. We let dlnorm() evaluate the log proposal density rather than hard-coding the simplified correction \(\sigma^\star / \sigma\), so that the same sampler works for any proposal we can draw from and evaluate.

propose_lognormal <- function(sigma) sigma * exp(rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 0.5))
log_q_lognormal <- function(to, from) dlnorm(to, meanlog = log(from), sdlog = 0.5, log = TRUE)

set.seed(84735)
fit_sigma <- metropolis_hastings(log_posterior_sigma, init = 1, n_iter = 10000,
                                 propose = propose_lognormal,
                                 log_q = log_q_lognormal)
fit_sigma$accept_rate
#> [1] 0.3624









Figure 7.4: Metropolis–Hastings with a log-Normal proposal for the standard deviation of sleep hours. Left: trace of the chain. Right: histogram of the draws after 500 warm-up iterations, with the posterior density overlaid. With the Hastings correction the histogram sits on the posterior.





The histogram in Figure 7.4 sits on the posterior density, where the histogram of the uncorrected sampler in Figure 7.2 did not. The two samplers use the same log-Normal proposal and differ only in the Hastings correction.

title: 7  The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm
text:
7.2 The independence sampler

7.2.1 A proposal that ignores the current state
An independence sampler draws every candidate from a fixed distribution that does not depend on the current state, i.e., \(q(\theta^\star \mid \theta) = q(\theta^\star)\). This distribution could be an approximation to the posterior or a conjugate posterior derived from a simpler model. In this case, the acceptance ratio simplifies to \[
r = \frac{f(\theta^\star)}{f(\theta^{(t)})} \times \frac{q(\theta^{(t)})}{q(\theta^\star)}
  = \frac{f(\theta^\star) / q(\theta^\star)}{f(\theta^{(t)}) / q(\theta^{(t)})}
  = \frac{w(\theta^\star)}{w(\theta^{(t)})}, \qquad w(\theta) = \frac{f(\theta)}{q(\theta)}.
\] The weight \(w(\theta)\) is large where the target density is high relative to the proposal density, and small where it is low. A candidate is accepted with certainty when its weight exceeds that of the current state, and otherwise with probability \(w(\theta^\star) / w(\theta^{(t)})\).
If the proposal exactly matches the posterior, \(w(\theta)\) has the same value for every \(\theta\). The ratio \(w(\theta^\star)/w(\theta^{(t)})\) is then always one, every candidate is accepted, and the chain produces independent posterior draws. When the proposal closely resembles the posterior, \(w\) varies little, so acceptance probabilities tend to be high. Because candidates are drawn independently of the current state, the resulting draws can also be much less correlated than those of a random walk.


Quiz yourself!

An independence sampler is at a state with weight \(w(\theta^{(t)}) = 2\) and draws a candidate with weight \(w(\theta^\star) = 0.5\). With what probability is the candidate accepted? And if the two weights were the other way around?



7.2.2 A Normal proposal for the Normal–Cauchy posterior
In Chapter 5, we estimated the average hours of sleep \(\mu\) with \(\sigma = 1\) known, using two different prior distributions. With the \(\text{N}(7, 0.5^2)\) prior, the posterior is exactly \(\text{N}(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)\). With the \(\text{Cauchy}(7, 0.5)\) prior, the posterior has no closed form, and we sampled from it using a random walk. Figure 5.6 showed that the two posterior distributions nearly coincide for these data. We can therefore use the known Normal posterior as a proposal for the Cauchy-prior posterior.

n <- length(sleep_hours)
tau2_n <- 1 / (1 / 0.5^2 + n / 1^2)
mu_n <- tau2_n * (7 / 0.5^2 + sum(sleep_hours) / 1^2)
tau_n <- sqrt(tau2_n)

log_posterior_cauchy <- function(mu, y = sleep_hours) {
  sum(dnorm(y, mean = mu, sd = 1, log = TRUE)) +
    dcauchy(mu, location = 7, scale = 0.5, log = TRUE)
}

Before running the sampler, consider the weight function \(w(\mu) = f(\mu) / q(\mu)\), which determines the acceptance probability of each candidate. The target is proportional to the likelihood times the Cauchy prior, while the proposal is proportional to the same likelihood times the Normal prior. Thus, \[
\begin{aligned}
w(\mu)
= \frac{f(\mu)}{q(\mu)} &= \frac{f(y \mid \mu)\,f_{\text{Cauchy}}(\mu)}
{\frac{f(y \mid \mu)\,f_{\text{Normal}}(\mu)}{f_{\text{Normal}}(y)}}\\
&= f_{\text{Normal}}(y)\,
\frac{f_{\text{Cauchy}}(\mu)}{f_{\text{Normal}}(\mu)}\\
&\propto \frac{f_{\text{Cauchy}}(\mu)}{f_{\text{Normal}}(\mu)},
\end{aligned}
\] where \(f_{\text{Cauchy}}(\mu)\) is the Cauchy\((7\text{, }0.5)\) density evaluated at \(\mu\) and \(f_{\text{Normal}}(\mu)\) the Normal\((7\text{, }0.5)\) density evaluated at \(\mu\). The likelihood cancels, leaving the ratio of the two prior densities multiplied by the normalizing constant \(f_{\text{Normal}}(y)\). This constant does not depend on \(\mu\) and cancels when we compute the acceptance ratio \(w(\mu^\star)/w(\mu^{(t)})\). Figure 7.5 shows the weight function over the region containing most of the posterior probability.








Figure 7.5: The weight function \(w(\mu) = f(\mu)/q(\mu)\) of the independence sampler for the Cauchy-prior posterior with the Normal–Normal posterior as proposal, scaled to equal one at the posterior mean (purple). The gray curve is the rescaled proposal density. The weight varies relatively little where the proposal places most of its probability but increases in the tails.





The Normal proposal closely resembles the Cauchy-prior posterior over the range of values where most of the posterior probability lies. Consequently, the ratio \(w(\mu) = f(\mu)/q(\mu)\) changes little across this range. The weights of the proposed and current values will usually be similar, giving acceptance probabilities close to one. We therefore expect a high acceptance rate.
We can now run the sampler. Because the proposal does not depend on the current state, propose() ignores its argument and log_q() ignores from.

set.seed(84735)
fit_indep <- metropolis_hastings(log_posterior_cauchy, init = 6.7, n_iter = 10000,
                                 propose = \(mu) rnorm(1, mu_n, tau_n),
                                 log_q = \(to, from) dnorm(to, mu_n, tau_n, log = TRUE))
c(accept_rate = fit_indep$accept_rate, ess = ess_basic(fit_indep$draws$theta))
#> accept_rate         ess 
#>       0.959    8009.340

The observed acceptance rate is 0.96, and the effective sample size is 8009 out of \(10{,}000\) iterations. We compare this with the random walk of Chapter 5 on the same posterior, using its hand-tuned step size of \(0.5\).

set.seed(84735)
fit_walk <- metropolis(log_posterior_cauchy, init = 6.7, n_iter = 10000, step_size = 0.5)
c(accept_rate = fit_walk$accept_rate, ess = ess_basic(fit_walk$draws$theta))
#> accept_rate         ess 
#>      0.4444   2284.3020

The random walk produces about 2284 effective draws from the same number of iterations, the independence sampler 4 times as many. Nearly every candidate comes from a distribution close to the posterior, and nearly every one is accepted.


7.2.3 Why a high acceptance rate is good news here
In Chapter 5 we warned that an acceptance rate of \(99\%\) is bad news for a random walk, and in Chapter 6 we built a sampler that deliberately aims for \(44\%\). Now we are celebrating 96%.
For a random walk, a very high acceptance rate usually means that the steps are too small. Almost every proposal is accepted, but the chain moves slowly through the posterior. The target of \(0.44\) balances step size against acceptance probability. For an independence sampler, candidates do not depend on the current state. Each is a fresh draw from \(q\), and if \(q\) resembles the posterior closely, most candidates have high acceptance probabilities. When nearly every candidate is accepted, the chain behaves much like a sequence of independent draws from the proposal. A high acceptance rate is therefore good news for an independence sampler.


Quiz yourself!

In Chapter 5 you told a colleague that a 99% acceptance rate was bad news. Now a different colleague reports a 98% acceptance rate for an independence sampler. Is it bad news this time? What does the rate tell you about the proposal?

title: 7  The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm
text:
7.3 More general proposals
We have seen two proposals beyond the Normal random walk, one that respects the support of a parameter and one that approximates the posterior. Any proposal that can reach the whole support of the target will do, as long as the Hastings correction is in the acceptance ratio. Later chapters build three more on the same foundation.
Proposals from conditional distributions. Chapter 8 (Gibbs Sampling and Metropolis-within-Gibbs) updates one parameter at a time by drawing from its conditional distribution given all the others. This is a special case of Metropolis–Hastings in which the target and proposal terms cancel, so every candidate is accepted.
Proposals that change the model. In Chapter 9 (Bayesian Variable Selection), the state of the chain includes which predictors are in a regression. A proposal may add or remove a predictor, moving between models with different sets of coefficients. Using mixtures of mutually singular distributions, we can construct Metropolis–Hastings updates for these moves and account for their different proposal probabilities. The chain then explores the regression coefficients and the set of predictors at once.
Proposals that follow the shape of the posterior. A random walk proposes without using information about the shape of the posterior. When the gradient of the log posterior is available, it can guide proposals toward regions of higher density. These proposals are generally asymmetric and require a Hastings correction. Chapter 11 (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) introduces Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which uses gradients to construct trajectories through the posterior and a Metropolis acceptance step to correct for numerical approximation. Stan’s sampler works this way.

title: 7  The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm
text:
7.4 Chapter summary
This chapter removed the one restriction that the samplers of Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 shared, the symmetric proposal.

A Normal step on \(\log \sigma\) multiplies \(\sigma\) by a random positive factor. Its density on the \(\sigma\) scale follows from the change-of-variables formula with the Jacobian, which gives a log-Normal density that is asymmetric, with the ratio \(q(\sigma \mid \sigma^\star) / q(\sigma^\star \mid \sigma) = \sigma^\star / \sigma\).
An asymmetric proposal used with the Metropolis rule produces a chain with the wrong stationary distribution, because moves in the favored direction are accepted as if they were not favored. The log-Normal proposal for a standard deviation drifts toward small values. The chain is still a valid Markov chain, so \(\widehat{R}\) and the effective sample size cannot reveal the error.
Metropolis–Hastings repairs this with the Hastings correction \(q(\theta^{(t)} \mid \theta^\star) / q(\theta^\star \mid \theta^{(t)})\) in the acceptance ratio. Substituting the corrected acceptance probability into the detailed-balance equation gives an expression that is symmetric in the two states, so detailed balance holds for any proposal that can reach every part of the target. For a symmetric proposal the correction is one.
The independence sampler draws every candidate from a fixed proposal \(q\), and its acceptance ratio is the ratio of the weights \(w = f / q\) at the candidate and the current state. A proposal close to the posterior gives nearly independent draws; the Normal–Normal posterior as proposal for the Normal–Cauchy posterior accepts nearly everything and beats the tuned random walk several times over.
For an independence sampler a high acceptance rate is good, because it measures how well \(q\) agrees with \(f\), not how small the steps are. Every accepted candidate is a draw from a distribution close to the posterior that does not depend on the previous state.

title: 7  The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm
text:
7.5 Quiz answers
Quiz 1. Under the Metropolis rule the acceptance probability would be \(\min\{1, 0.10 / 0.40\} = 0.25\). The move is upward, and the correction for the log-Normal proposal is \(\sigma^\star / \sigma^{(t)} = 2\), so under Metropolis–Hastings \(r = 0.25 \times 2 = 0.5\) and the move is accepted with probability \(0.5\). The Metropolis rule under-accepts upward moves and over-accepts downward ones, which is how the uncorrected chain drifts toward small values.
Quiz 2. The acceptance ratio is \(r = w(\theta^\star) / w(\theta^{(t)}) = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25\), so the candidate is accepted with probability \(0.25\). With the weights the other way around, \(r = 2 / 0.5 = 4 \geq 1\) and the candidate is accepted for certain.
Quiz 3. No. For an independence sampler the acceptance rate does not measure the size of the moves, because every candidate is a fresh draw from the proposal wherever the chain is. A rate of 98% means that \(w = f/q\) is nearly constant over the region where the chain lives, that is, the proposal is nearly the posterior, and the draws are nearly independent.

title: 7  The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm
text:
7.6 Exercises

7.6.1 Conceptual exercises

Exercise 7.1 (Correcting for asymmetry) A chain is at \(\theta^{(t)} = 2\), and the proposal produces \(\theta^\star = 3\). The unnormalized target is \(f(2) = 0.8\) and \(f(3) = 0.4\). Compute the acceptance probability for each proposal distribution below.

A symmetric proposal, \(\theta^\star \sim \text{N}(\theta^{(t)}, 1)\).
A log-Normal proposal, \(\theta^\star = \theta^{(t)} e^{\varepsilon}\) with \(\varepsilon \sim \text{N}(0, 0.25)\).
An independence proposal, \(\theta^\star \sim \text{Exponential}(1)\).
A proposal that always moves one unit to the right, \(\theta^\star = \theta^{(t)} + 1\). What goes wrong, and what does it tell you about the requirement that \(q\) can be evaluated in both directions?



Exercise 7.2 (The prior as proposal) Consider an independence sampler whose proposal is the prior, \(q(\theta) = f(\theta)\), for a posterior \(f(\theta \mid y) \propto f(y \mid \theta) f(\theta)\).

Show that the acceptance ratio is the likelihood ratio \(f(y \mid \theta^\star) / f(y \mid \theta^{(t)})\).
Explain, in terms of the weight function \(w\), why it becomes less and less efficient as the sample size grows. Compare with the Normal–Normal proposal in the text, where the likelihood cancelled from \(w\) instead of being all of it.



Exercise 7.3 (A proposal that drifts) A chain for a parameter on the real line uses the proposal \(\theta^\star \sim \text{N}(\theta^{(t)} + 0.5, 1)\), which is a random walk with a drift to the right.

Write down \(q(\theta^\star \mid \theta)\) and \(q(\theta \mid \theta^\star)\) and simplify their ratio.
A chain is at \(\theta^{(t)} = 0\) and proposes \(\theta^\star = 1\); the target satisfies \(f(1) = f(0)\). What is the acceptance probability under Metropolis–Hastings, and what would it be under the uncorrected Metropolis rule?
Describe what the uncorrected chain would do in the long run.




7.6.2 Practical exercises

Exercise 7.4 (Gen X with a Beta proposal) Return to the Gen X proportion of Chapter 2, with the \(\text{Beta}(4, 6)\) prior and the moma_sample data, whose posterior is \(\text{Beta}(4 + y, 6 + 100 - y)\). Pretend you do not know this, and build independence samplers with Beta proposals.

Use the prior as the proposal. Report the acceptance rate and the effective sample size, and explain the acceptance rate in terms of the likelihood.
Run adaptive_metropolis() on the logit scale \(\psi = \text{logit}\,\pi\) for 2,000 iterations as a pilot, adding the log Jacobian \(\log \pi + \log(1 - \pi)\) of Chapter 2 to the log target. Compute the mean \(m\) and variance \(v\) of the back-transformed draws plogis(psi), and use the \(\text{Beta}(m k, (1 - m) k)\) proposal with \(k = m(1 - m)/v - 1\), which has the same mean and variance. Report the acceptance rate and the effective sample size.



Exercise 7.5 (A log-Normal proposal for a rate) Return to the Gamma-Poisson model of Exercise 5.5: a Poisson rate \(\lambda\) with a \(\text{Gamma}(3, 1)\) prior and data \(y = (2, 0, 4, 1, 3, 2)\).

Sample \(\lambda\) with metropolis_hastings() and the log-Normal proposal with \(c = 0.5\) for 10,000 iterations. Compare the posterior mean and standard deviation with the exact Gamma posterior.
Delete the Hastings correction from the sampler in part a, rerun, and compare with the exact posterior. In which direction is the error, and why?



Exercise 7.6 (Adapting the log-Normal proposal) Return to the posterior of \(\sigma\) for the sleep hours. Write adaptive_metropolis_hastings(), which takes log_target, init, n_iter, a proposal function and a log proposal density that both take the step size as an extra argument, and adapts the log step size by the rule of Equation 6.2 during a warm-up of n_adapt iterations before freezing it, aiming for an acceptance rate of \(0.44\). Base it on the final adaptive_metropolis() of Chapter 6.

Use the log-Normal proposal, with the step size as the standard deviation of \(\varepsilon\). Run \(10{,}000\) iterations from \(\sigma = 1\) with a starting step size of \(5\), and report the frozen step size and the acceptance rate after the freeze.
Compare the posterior mean and standard deviation of the kept draws with the values obtained by numerical integration of the unnormalized posterior with integrate().
Repeat from a starting step size of \(0.01\). Do the two runs freeze at the same step size? What does that tell you that the acceptance rate does not?
Explain why the adaptation rule of Chapter 6 needed no change for an asymmetric proposal, and why the chain after the freeze is covered by the argument of this chapter.




7.6.3 Applied exercises

Exercise 7.7 (Do Americans believe in ghosts?) The pulse_of_the_nation data in the bayesrules package record, among other things, whether each of 1,000 respondents believes in ghosts. Let \(\pi\) be the proportion of believers in the population, with a \(\text{Beta}(2, 2)\) prior, and work on the logit scale \(\psi = \text{logit}\, \pi\), adding the log Jacobian \(\log \pi + \log(1 - \pi)\) of Chapter 2 to the log target.

Run adaptive_metropolis() on the logit scale for 4,000 iterations as a pilot, and compute the mean and standard deviation of the kept draws of \(\psi\).
Build an independence sampler on the logit scale whose proposal is a Normal with that mean and standard deviation. Report the acceptance rate and the effective sample size, and compare with the pilot.
Run the independence sampler with the \(\text{Beta}(2, 2)\) prior as the proposal. Why does it do so much worse for this data set than the prior did for the Gen X example in Exercise 7.4?



Exercise 7.8 (Two ADHD symptoms, with a bivariate proposal) Return to the logistic regression of Exercise 6.9 for distract on avoid in the ADHD data of the bgms package, with independent \(\text{N}(0, 2^2)\) priors on \((\beta_0, \beta_1)\).

Run adaptive_metropolis() for 10,000 iterations as a pilot, and compute the mean vector and covariance matrix of the kept draws.
Build an independence sampler whose proposal is the bivariate Normal with that mean and covariance, using mvtnorm::rmvnorm() and mvtnorm::dmvnorm(). Report the acceptance rate and the effective sample size of each coefficient, and compare with the pilot.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.1 R and RStudio
The examples in this book run in R. Packages help with data, plots, and diagnostics, while you implement many of the samplers yourself. Fitting a Stan model also requires a C++ compiler. This appendix explains how to install the software, test a small model, and identify where to look if the test fails.
If you already use R and Stan on this computer, begin with the test in Section A.4. A successful run confirms that this example can compile and sample in your current installation. If a package or compiler is missing, return to the relevant setup step below.
Install R first and RStudio second; RStudio is an editor and needs R to be there already.
Both are free. Quarto, which we use to build this book, ships inside RStudio; you do not need it for the course.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
R. Download a current release from CRAN using the link for your operating system. On Windows, use the Windows installer. On macOS, choose the installer for your processor (Apple silicon or Intel). On Linux, follow CRAN’s instructions for your distribution. If R is already installed, R.version.string reports its version; older installations may need an update to install current packages.
RStudio. Install RStudio Desktop for the same operating system. RStudio provides an editor, console, and tools for managing your R work.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.2 R packages
The following packages cover Chapters 1–5 and the installation checks in this appendix. On Linux, complete the compiler setup in Section A.3 before installing R packages from source. Run the installation block once in the R console. Later, use library() to load the packages listed at the start of the chapter you are studying.

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",  # data handling and plotting
  "bayesrules", # course data sets
  "patchwork",  # combining plots
  "mvtnorm",    # multivariate Normal densities and draws
  "posterior",  # draws objects, ESS, R-hat, and MCSE
  "bayesplot",  # plots of simulation output
  "rstan",      # fitting Stan models from R
  "knitr",      # displaying tables in the examples
  "pkgbuild"    # checking the compiler setup
))

Packages that these depend on, such as dplyr, tidyr, and scales, are installed automatically. For the later chapters, also install

install.packages(c(
  "lars",     # diabetes data, Chapters 7–9
  "bgms",     # graphical-model examples, Chapters 7–9
  "numDeriv"  # numerical gradient checks, Chapter 11
))

On Windows and macOS, CRAN usually provides precompiled packages for current supported R versions. On Linux, packages are commonly compiled from source. Installing rstan and compiling a Stan model are separate steps: even with a precompiled R package, fitting your own Stan model requires a C++ compiler.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.3 Installing Stan
rstan is the R interface to Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017). The Stan program you write is translated to C++ and compiled, so you need a compiler that R knows how to call. What that means depends on your operating system.
macOS. Install the Xcode Command Line Tools by opening the Terminal app and running
xcode-select --install
This installs the Command Line Tools, the smaller toolset containing the compiler and other command-line utilities. You do not need the full Xcode application. If the tools are already installed, the command reports this.
Windows. Install Rtools using the version recommended for your installed R version. Check R.version.string first and follow the matching link on the Rtools page. Use the default installation location unless your institution provides different instructions.
Linux. Install a C++ compiler, make, and R’s development files. On Debian and Ubuntu, these are supplied by build-essential and r-base-dev. Other distributions use different package names; follow their R installation instructions. The RStan installation guide links to platform-specific toolchain instructions.
On all three platforms, restart R after installing the toolchain, and confirm that R can see it:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

A result of TRUE indicates that the build-tools check succeeded. If it returns FALSE, inspect the diagnostic messages and the instructions for your platform before attempting the model below. This check helps locate compiler problems; compiling the actual Stan model is the next test.


Stan settings used in the examples


library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = 1)

auto_write = TRUE allows RStan to reuse saved compiled models. mc.cores = 1 runs the chains one after another, as in the setup for Chapter 4. Multiple chains still run; this setting controls how many can run at the same time. On a suitably configured computer, a larger value allows parallel chains.

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
Appendix A — Software Setup
section: A.5 If rstan will not compile
text:
A.5 If rstan will not compile
If the compiler check succeeds but RStan still fails to compile, consult the platform-specific RStan guide using the complete error message. On a managed computer, installation changes may require help from your university’s support service.
An alternative is cmdstanr, another R interface to Stan. It uses a separate CmdStan installation, so it can avoid some RStan-specific compiler-configuration problems. It still needs a working C++ toolchain. The CmdStanR getting-started guide gives the installation steps:

install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos")))
library(cmdstanr)
check_cmdstan_toolchain()
install_cmdstan(cores = 2)
cmdstan_version()

On Windows, check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE) can attempt to configure missing toolchain components; this option does not repair macOS or Linux installations. Follow the compiler instructions for your platform first.
To fit the same test model with CmdStanR, use the bb_model and bb_data objects defined above:

mod <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(bb_model))
fit_cmdstan <- mod$sample(
  data = bb_data, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 1,
  iter_warmup = 1000, iter_sampling = 1000, seed = 84735)

RStan’s iter = 2000 includes warm-up. CmdStanR specifies the 1,000 warm-up and 1,000 retained iterations separately. Its fitted object also has different methods: for example, fit_cmdstan$summary() gives its summary table.
For the diagnostic workflow in Chapter 4, convert either fitted object to the draws format used by posterior and bayesplot. With RStan:

draws <- posterior::as_draws_array(as.array(fit))

With CmdStanR:

draws <- fit_cmdstan$draws()

Both draws objects can then be used with functions such as posterior::summarise_draws() and bayesplot::mcmc_trace(draws, pars = "pi").

title: Appendix A — Software Setup
text:
A.6 Reproducibility: seeds and sessions
Examples that generate random draws use seeds so that you can repeat the calculation. R and Stan have separate random number generators.
R’s seed. Run the package setup and any earlier code that defines the data and functions needed for an example. In Chapters 1–5, the simulation chunks set their own seed before drawing random numbers. Rerunning one of these chunks therefore restarts its random sequence. Follow the seed shown in the example; some illustrations deliberately use a different value.
The following two calls produce the same values because we reset the seed between them:

set.seed(84735)
first <- rnorm(3)
set.seed(84735)
second <- rnorm(3)
rbind(first = first, second = second)

            [,1]       [,2]      [,3]
first  0.6672327 -0.1238403 0.7808676
second 0.6672327 -0.1238403 0.7808676

identical(first, second)

[1] TRUE


Resetting a seed at the start of an example is different from resetting it inside a sampler’s iteration loop. Inside the loop, the reset would repeatedly generate the same numbers and change the sampling procedure. The R random-number documentation explains how set.seed() controls the generator.
Stan’s seed. set.seed() does not set Stan’s generator. Supply seed = to stan() or the CmdStanR $sample() method, as in the examples above. Exact reproduction also depends on the model, data, initialization, chain configuration, software, and computing environment; see the Stan reproducibility documentation. Small differences across installations are possible even with the same seed. Compare posterior summaries with their Monte Carlo uncertainty rather than expecting every saved value to match.
A reproducible calculation can still contain an error. When assessing a sampler, also try other seeds and starting values, and use the diagnostics in Chapter 4.
Finally, when you report a problem or hand in an assignment, include the output of sessionInfo(). It lists your R version, your operating system, and the version of every loaded package, which is usually the first thing anyone helping you will ask for.

sessionInfo()



Setup checklist


R and RStudio installed for your operating system.
The packages needed for your chapters installed; the chapter’s setup code loaded.
A working C++ toolchain for Stan: Command Line Tools on macOS, matching Rtools on Windows, or the appropriate compiler and R development packages on Linux.
The Beta-Binomial test model compiles and runs, with an estimated mean near 0.667 and its output and warnings inspected.
Seeds supplied separately for R and Stan; sessionInfo() available when reporting a problem.






Carpenter, B., Gelman, A., Hoffman, M. D., Lee, D., Goodrich, B., Betancourt, M., Brubaker, M., Guo, J., Li, P., & Riddell, A. (2017). Stan: A probabilistic programming language. Journal of Statistical Software, 76(1), 1–32.

title: Appendix B — Notation
text:
B.1 Conventions
This appendix collects the symbols used for data, probability distributions, Markov chains, and sampling algorithms throughout the book.
Probability functions. We write \(f(\cdot)\) for probability mass functions and densities. The arguments distinguish the prior \(f(\theta)\), the likelihood contribution \(f(y\mid\theta)\), and the posterior \(f(\theta\mid y)\). In descriptions of a sampler, \(f(\theta)\) can instead denote the chosen target density. A proportion parameter is written \(\pi\); the proposal density has its own symbol \(q\).
Work on the log scale. Where a sampler takes a target-density function, we supply its logarithm, typically called log_target or log_posterior. Products of many small likelihood contributions can round to zero; logarithms let us add their values instead. A log density ratio is a difference, \(\log r=\log f(\theta^\star)-\log f(\theta^{(t)})\), and the acceptance test becomes \(\log u<\log r\) (Chapter 5). R’s density functions can compute log densities directly with log = TRUE.
Vectors are bold, indices are subscripts, iterations are superscripts. A single parameter is \(\theta\); a vector of parameters is \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_d)\); a matrix is a bold capital such as \(\mathbf{P}\) or \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). Observations are indexed \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), predictors \(j = 1, \ldots, p\), and models \(m = 1, \ldots, M\). The state of a Markov chain at iteration \(t\) is \(\theta^{(t)}\), with parentheses so that it is not mistaken for a power; a proposed value is \(\theta^\star\). The starting state is indexed \(t=0\). A run recording \(N\) sampled states has updates \(t=1,\ldots,N\); summaries after warm-up use the retained states. Hats denote estimates computed from draws, as in \(\widehat{R}\).

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC
text:
C.1 The variance of a dependent average
These notes expand on the diagnostics in Chapter 4 and derive the acceptance rule used in Chapter 5 and Chapter 7. Exercise 4.7 uses the R-hat functions in Section C.2.
For \(N\) independent draws with variance \(\sigma^2\), the variance of their average is \(\sigma^2/N\). Dependent draws can vary together, so their covariances also contribute. We derive that contribution first for three states and then for a run of length \(N\).
Assume the chain is stationary, with the same mean and finite variance at every iteration. Write \(\rho_k\) for its autocorrelation at lag \(k\). Two states separated by \(k\) iterations then have covariance \[
\operatorname{Cov}(\theta^{(t)},\theta^{(t+k)})=\sigma^2\rho_k.
\] Stationarity makes this covariance depend on the separation \(k\), rather than on which iteration we start from.

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC
text:
C.1.1 Start with three sampled states
For \(N=3\), the average is \(\bar\theta=(\theta^{(1)}+\theta^{(2)}+\theta^{(3)})/3\). Dividing by three divides the variance by \(3^2=9\). The variance of a sum includes each individual variance and twice the covariance of each distinct pair: \[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)=\frac19\bigl[&
\operatorname{Var}(\theta^{(1)})+
\operatorname{Var}(\theta^{(2)})+
\operatorname{Var}(\theta^{(3)})\\
&+2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta^{(1)},\theta^{(2)})
+2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta^{(1)},\theta^{(3)})\\
&+2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta^{(2)},\theta^{(3)})\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\] The factor two comes from the cross-products when we square a sum, just as \((a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\).
There are two pairs one iteration apart: \((1,2)\) and \((2,3)\). Both have covariance \(\sigma^2\rho_1\). The remaining pair, \((1,3)\), is two iterations apart and has covariance \(\sigma^2\rho_2\). Substituting gives \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{9}\bigl(3+4\rho_1+2\rho_2\bigr).
\] For independent draws, both correlations are zero and we recover \(\sigma^2/3\). For the stationary AR(1) chain with \(\phi=0.5\) and target variance one, \(\rho_1=0.5\) and \(\rho_2=0.25\). The variance of the average is then \((3+4\times0.5+2\times0.25)/9\approx0.611\), compared with \(1/3\approx0.333\) for three independent draws. The positive correlations make the average more variable across repeated runs.


C.1.2 Count the pairs in a run of length \(N\)
For an average of \(N\) states, the same variance-of-a-sum calculation gives \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)
=\frac1{N^2}\left[
\sum_{t=1}^N\operatorname{Var}(\theta^{(t)})
+2\sum_{1\leq t<s\leq N}
\operatorname{Cov}(\theta^{(t)},\theta^{(s)})\right].
\] The second sum includes every distinct pair once. Group the pairs by their separation. At lag one there are \(N-1\) pairs; at lag two there are \(N-2\); at lag \(k\) there are \(N-k\). Every pair in that last group has covariance \(\sigma^2\rho_k\). Therefore \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)
=\frac1{N^2}\left[N\sigma^2
+2\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\rho_k\right].
\] Factoring out \(\sigma^2/N\) yields \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\left[1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}
\left(1-\frac{k}{N}\right)\rho_k\right].
\tag{C.1}\] This is the exact finite-run variance for the stationary chain. The weight \(1-k/N\) records that there are fewer pairs at longer lags. Substituting \(N=3\) reproduces the expression above.


C.1.3 Approximation for a long run
When \(N\) is large relative to the lags with appreciable correlation, the corresponding weights \(1-k/N\) are close to one. If correlations also become small fast enough that \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}|\rho_k|\) is finite, we can approximate the weighted finite sum by the infinite sum: \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar\theta)\approx\frac{\sigma^2}{N}
\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k\right).
\]
For an AR(1) chain with \(|\phi|<1\), \(\rho_k=\phi^k\). The geometric series gives \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\phi^k=\phi/(1-\phi)\), so \[
1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k
=1+\frac{2\phi}{1-\phi}
=\frac{1+\phi}{1-\phi}.
\] Equating this approximate variance to \(\sigma^2/N_{\mathrm{eff}}\) gives \[
N_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx N\frac{1-\phi}{1+\phi},
\] the AR(1) expression used in Chapter 4. Positive \(\phi\) reduces the effective sample size. Negative \(\phi\) can give \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}>N\) because alternating deviations can make the average more precise than an independent-sample average of the same length. Thinning can remove that benefit.

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC
section: C.2 Calculating basic and split R-hat
text:
C.2 Calculating basic and split R-hat
For \(m\) chains of length \(L\), let \(s_j^2\) and \(\bar\theta_j\) be the variance and mean within chain \(j\), and \(\bar\theta_{\cdot}\) the average of the chain means. Then \[
W=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m s_j^2,\qquad
B=\frac{L}{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^m(\bar\theta_j-\bar\theta_{\cdot})^2.
\] We illustrate the calculation with four records of independent standard Normal draws. The following functions implement the basic R-hat formula and split each column into equal-length first and last halves. For an odd number of values, the middle value is left out.

rhat_by_hand <- function(x) {
  L <- nrow(x)
  W <- mean(apply(x, 2, var))
  B <- L * var(colMeans(x))
  sqrt(((L - 1) / L * W + B / L) / W)
}
split_halves <- function(x) {
  half <- floor(nrow(x) / 2)
  cbind(x[seq_len(half), , drop = FALSE],
        x[seq.int(nrow(x) - half + 1, nrow(x)), , drop = FALSE])
}
set.seed(48407)
normal_chains <- matrix(rnorm(4000), ncol = 4)
rbind(
  unsplit = c(by_hand = rhat_by_hand(normal_chains),
              package = rhat_basic(normal_chains, split = FALSE)),
  split = c(by_hand = rhat_by_hand(split_halves(normal_chains)),
            package = rhat_basic(normal_chains, split = TRUE))
)
#>          by_hand  package
#> unsplit 1.000113 1.000113
#> split   1.000048 1.000048

Within each row, the hand and package calculations match because they implement the same formula. The split and unsplit results can also look nearly identical after rounding when both halves explore similar values. rhat_basic() splits by default; split = FALSE disables that step.

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC
text:
C.3 Rank normalization and folding
Chains can agree about their center and still disagree about their spread. Suppose two records vary narrowly around zero while two others range much farther above and below it. Their means can be similar, so comparing means alone may give little warning.
The following code creates that situation. All four records have an expected mean of zero, but the last two have standard deviation three instead of one:

set.seed(48408)
same_mean <- cbind(rnorm(1000, 0, 1), rnorm(1000, 0, 1), rnorm(1000, 0, 3), rnorm(1000, 0, 3))
c(basic = rhat_basic(same_mean), rank_normalized = posterior::rhat(same_mean))
#>           basic rank_normalized 
#>        1.000529        1.187145

posterior::rhat() adds two improvements to the basic split calculation (Vehtari et al., 2021).
Rank normalization replaces values by their positions in an ordered list. For example, the values \((-3,-1,1,3)\) have ranks \((1,2,3,4)\). An extremely large value still receives the highest rank, but its numerical size no longer dominates the comparison.
After splitting the chains, we rank all their retained values together. Ties receive their average rank. We then convert the ranks to standard Normal scores. If \(r\) is a rank and \(S\) the total number of ranked values, the transformation is \[
z=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{r-3/8}{S+1/4}\right).
\] The expression inside \(\Phi^{-1}\) turns a rank into a probability between zero and one; \(\Phi^{-1}\) gives the corresponding standard Normal quantile. For the four-value example, the scores are approximately \((-1.05,-0.30,0.30,1.05)\). We calculate basic R-hat on the scores. This makes the comparison less sensitive to extreme values, including those from distributions with very long tails. Bulk ESS uses this same transformation of the split chains before estimating ESS. Tail ESS instead computes ESS for indicators of falling below the pooled 5% quantile and below the pooled 95% quantile, and reports the smaller value.
Folding checks spread more directly. Replace each original value by its distance from the pooled median. In the four-value example the median is zero, so \((-3,-1,1,3)\) becomes \((3,1,1,3)\). The sign disappears and distance from the center remains. Wider chains now tend to have larger values than narrower chains. We split and rank-normalize these distances, then calculate R-hat again.
The reported posterior::rhat() is the larger of these two results. Figure C.1 shows how folding separates records with different spreads. In this example, ranking the original values alone can miss the problem, while folding reveals it. The code below calculates both parts and compares their maximum with posterior::rhat():

rank_normalize <- function(x) {
  ranks <- rank(x, ties.method = "average")
  scores <- qnorm((ranks - 3/8) / (length(ranks) + 1/4))
  matrix(scores, nrow = nrow(x), ncol = ncol(x))
}
rank_component <- rhat_by_hand(rank_normalize(split_halves(same_mean)))
folded <- abs(same_mean - median(same_mean))
fold_component <- rhat_by_hand(rank_normalize(split_halves(folded)))
c(rank_component = rank_component, folded_component = fold_component,
  maximum = max(rank_component, fold_component), package = posterior::rhat(same_mean))
#>   rank_component folded_component          maximum          package 
#>         1.000340         1.187145         1.187145         1.187145









Figure C.1: Folding makes a spread difference easier to compare. Left: records share a center but have different spreads. Right: absolute deviations from the pooled median are systematically larger in the wider records.

title: Appendix C — Technical Notes on MCMC
section: C.4 Deriving the Metropolis acceptance probability
text:
C.4 Deriving the Metropolis acceptance probability
The Metropolis rule accepts every proposal to a higher target density and only some proposals to a lower one. How do we obtain these probabilities? We can choose them by solving the detailed balance equation (van den Bergh et al., 2026, Appendix B).
Let \(a\) be the current state and \(b\) a proposed state. Write \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}\) for the probability of accepting the move from \(a\) to \(b\), and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}}\) for the acceptance probability if we instead propose \(a\) from \(b\). These are probabilities for two possible directions, not two decisions made in one iteration. For this derivation, assume that both states have positive, finite target density and that the proposal densities in both directions are positive.

C.4.1 Relating the two directions
Detailed balance is satisfied when \[
f(a)q(b\mid a)\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}
=f(b)q(a\mid b)\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}}.
\tag{C.2}\] For the symmetric proposals in Chapter 5, \(q(b\mid a)=q(a\mid b)\), so these factors cancel. Dividing by \(f(a)\) leaves \[
\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}=r\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}},
\qquad r=\frac{f(b)}{f(a)}.
\tag{C.3}\] Once we choose an acceptance probability in one direction, this equation fixes the probability in the other. The choices must also lie between zero and one.
Since \(\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}}\leq1\), the equation gives \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}\leq r\). We also require \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}\leq1\). The largest permitted forward probability is therefore \(\min(1,r)\). Taking this value gives the Metropolis rule: \[
\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}=\min(1,r),
\qquad
\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}}=\min(1,1/r).
\tag{C.4}\]
If \(r<1\), set \(\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}}=1\) and obtain \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}=r\). The proposal goes to a lower target density, so it is accepted only sometimes. If \(r\geq1\), set \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}=1\) and obtain \(\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}}=1/r\). The proposal goes to an equal or higher target density and is always accepted. In either case, the equation is satisfied in both directions. Proposals outside the target support are rejected.


C.4.2 A numerical comparison
Suppose \(f(a)=0.2\), \(f(b)=0.1\), and the symmetric proposal density is 0.3 in either direction. Then \(r=0.5\). The two sides of Equation C.2 are \[
\underbrace{0.2\times0.3\times0.5}_{a\text{ to }b}
=\underbrace{0.1\times0.3\times1}_{b\text{ to }a}
=0.03.
\] The target assigns a higher density to \(a\), but the smaller acceptance probability from \(a\) to \(b\) compensates for that difference.
There are other balanced choices. For example, \(\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}=0.25\) and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}}=0.5\) also satisfy Equation C.3, since \(0.25=0.5\times0.5\). Both sides of the balance equation then equal 0.015. Both directions would produce more rejections. The Metropolis choice makes both acceptance probabilities as large as possible while preserving their required relationship; detailed balance alone does not specify a unique rule.


C.4.3 Allowing asymmetric proposals
When proposal densities differ between directions, retain them in Equation C.2. The same rearrangement gives \[
\alpha_{\mathrm{fwd}}=R\alpha_{\mathrm{rev}},
\qquad
R=\frac{f(b)q(a\mid b)}{f(a)q(b\mid a)}.
\] Applying the same bounds yields the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability \[
\alpha(a,b)=\min\!\left\{1,
\frac{f(b)q(a\mid b)}{f(a)q(b\mid a)}\right\}.
\tag{C.5}\] The reverse proposal density is in the numerator and the forward proposal density is in the denominator. This adjustment accounts for a proposal mechanism that favors one direction. Chapter 7 develops examples of such proposals. With a symmetric proposal, their ratio is one and the expression reduces to the rule derived above.




van den Bergh, D., Clyde, M. A., Raftery, A. E., & Marsman, M. (2026). Reversible jump MCMC with no regrets: Bayesian variable selection using mixtures of mutually singular distributions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27791


Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., Simpson, D., Carpenter, B., & Bürkner, P.-C. (2021). Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved \(\widehat{R}\) for assessing convergence of MCMC (with discussion). Bayesian Analysis, 16(2), 667–718.

title: Appendix D — Deriving Conjugate Posteriors
text:
D.1 What we need to recognize
In the modern art example in Chapter 2, a Beta prior and a Binomial likelihood give a Beta posterior. The same kind of calculation gives the other two updates in Table 2.1. Here we work through all three, beginning with the probability functions and ending with the posterior parameters.
Bayes’ rule says that the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. To identify its distribution, we first keep all the factors that depend on the unknown parameter. Their product is a kernel: it gives the shape of a density without necessarily including the constant that makes its integral equal to one.
For example, multiplying a function of \(\pi\) by 10 changes its height at every \(\pi\) by the same factor. Once we divide by its integral, that factor cancels. Multiplying by \(\pi\), however, changes the relative heights at different values of \(\pi\) and therefore changes the distribution. This is why we can set aside factors that are constant with respect to the parameter, but must retain factors that vary with it.
We then compare the kernel with a familiar density on the same range of possible parameter values. If they match, the familiar density supplies both the distribution’s name and its normalizing constant. On the log scale, constant factors become additive terms. We write these as \(C\), allowing its value to change as we collect terms. Such constants may depend on the observed data; they must not depend on the parameter whose posterior we are finding.
The constants can be set aside when identifying the posterior. Computing the marginal likelihood requires the full likelihood and prior, including their constants, as in the model comparisons in Chapter 2.

title: Appendix D — Deriving Conjugate Posteriors
section: D.2 A Binomial likelihood and a Beta prior
text:
D.2 A Binomial likelihood and a Beta prior
Let \(y\) be the observed number of successes in \(n\) trials, with common success probability \(\pi\). Under the Binomial model, \[
f(y\mid\pi)=\binom{n}{y}\pi^y(1-\pi)^{n-y},
\qquad 0<\pi<1.
\] Here \(n\) and \(y\) are known. The factor \(\binom{n}{y}\) counts how many trial sequences give \(y\) successes; it does not change as we vary \(\pi\).
Assign \(\pi\) a \(\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) prior, with \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta>0\). Its density is \[
f(\pi)=\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\pi^{\alpha-1}(1-\pi)^{\beta-1},
\qquad 0<\pi<1.
\] The Beta function \(B(\alpha,\beta)\) is the integral of \(\pi^{\alpha-1}(1-\pi)^{\beta-1}\) over \((0,1)\). Dividing by it makes the prior integrate to one. Since \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are fixed prior parameters, it too is constant with respect to \(\pi\).
Multiplying the likelihood and prior, and setting aside these constant factors, gives \[
\begin{aligned}
f(\pi\mid y)
&\propto \pi^y(1-\pi)^{n-y}
          \pi^{\alpha-1}(1-\pi)^{\beta-1}\\
&=\pi^{\alpha+y-1}(1-\pi)^{\beta+n-y-1}.
\end{aligned}
\] The second line uses the rule that exponents add when we multiply powers with the same base. The \(y\) successes add \(y\) to the exponent of \(\pi\); the \(n-y\) failures add \(n-y\) to the exponent of \(1-\pi\).
A Beta density with parameters \(a\) and \(b\) has exponents \(a-1\) and \(b-1\). Matching them gives \(a=\alpha+y\) and \(b=\beta+n-y\). The range is still \((0,1)\), so \[
\pi\mid y\sim\text{Beta}(\alpha+y,\;\beta+n-y).
\] We can now write the normalized posterior explicitly: \[
f(\pi\mid y)=
\frac{\pi^{\alpha+y-1}(1-\pi)^{\beta+n-y-1}}
{B(\alpha+y,\beta+n-y)},
\qquad 0<\pi<1.
\] The denominator uses the updated parameters. Reusing the prior’s normalizing constant would not make this new density integrate to one.
For the modern art data, \(\alpha=4\), \(\beta=6\), \(n=100\), and \(y=14\). The posterior is therefore \(\text{Beta}(18,92)\). Its mean is \(18/(18+92)\approx0.164\), between the prior mean \(0.4\) and the sample proportion \(0.14\). More generally, for \(n>0\), \[
E[\pi\mid y]
=\frac{\alpha+y}{\alpha+\beta+n}
=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+n}
  \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
+\frac{n}{\alpha+\beta+n}\frac{y}{n}.
\] The last expression is a weighted average of the prior mean and the sample proportion. The weights add to one, and the data receive more weight as \(n\) increases while the prior stays fixed.

title: Appendix D — Deriving Conjugate Posteriors
section: D.3 A Poisson likelihood and a Gamma prior
text:
D.3 A Poisson likelihood and a Gamma prior
Now suppose \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) are counts from \(n\) observation periods of equal length. We model them as independent given a common expected count \(\lambda\): \[
Y_i\mid\lambda\sim\text{Pois}(\lambda),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\] For a single observation, the probability is \(\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}/y_i!\). Conditional independence lets us multiply these probabilities to obtain the joint likelihood: \[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf y\mid\lambda)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}\\
&=\frac{\lambda^{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}e^{-n\lambda}}
         {\prod_{i=1}^n y_i!}.
\end{aligned}
\] There are two combinations to notice. Multiplying the powers of \(\lambda\) adds the observed counts in the exponent. Multiplying \(n\) copies of \(e^{-\lambda}\) gives \(e^{-n\lambda}\). The factorials in the denominator involve only the observed counts, so the likelihood kernel is \[
\lambda^{\sum_i y_i}e^{-n\lambda},\qquad \lambda>0.
\]
Use a \(\text{Gamma}(s,r)\) prior with shape \(s>0\) and rate \(r>0\): \[
f(\lambda)=\frac{r^s}{\Gamma(s)}\lambda^{s-1}e^{-r\lambda},
\qquad \lambda>0.
\] Here \(\Gamma(s)\) is the Gamma function; together with \(r^s\) it supplies the normalizing constant. To recognize the distribution we need the power \(s-1\) and the coefficient \(r\) in the exponential. The rate convention matters: a Gamma density written using a scale parameter would instead have \(e^{-\lambda/\text{scale}}\).
Multiplying the two kernels gives \[
\begin{aligned}
f(\lambda\mid\mathbf y)
&\propto \lambda^{\sum_i y_i}e^{-n\lambda}
          \lambda^{s-1}e^{-r\lambda}\\
&=\lambda^{s+\sum_i y_i-1}e^{-(r+n)\lambda}.
\end{aligned}
\] This has the Gamma form again: the shape is \(s+\sum_i y_i\), and the rate is \(r+n\). Thus \[
\lambda\mid\mathbf y\sim
\text{Gamma}\!\left(s+\sum_{i=1}^n y_i,\;r+n\right).
\] The sum of the counts updates the shape; the number of observation periods updates the rate. Substituting these two parameters into the Gamma density above gives the normalized posterior: \[
f(\lambda\mid\mathbf y)
=\frac{(r+n)^{s+\sum_i y_i}}{\Gamma(s+\sum_i y_i)}
\lambda^{s+\sum_i y_i-1}e^{-(r+n)\lambda},
\qquad \lambda>0.
\]
For example, suppose four equal-length task sessions produce counts of \(2,0,3,1\) attention lapses, and we use a \(\text{Gamma}(2,1)\) prior for the expected count per session. There are \(n=4\) sessions and \(\sum_i y_i=6\) lapses, giving a \(\text{Gamma}(8,5)\) posterior. The prior mean is \(2/1=2\), the observed average is \(6/4=1.5\), and the posterior mean is \(8/5=1.6\).
The weighted-average interpretation is visible algebraically as well: \[
E[\lambda\mid\mathbf y]
=\frac{s+\sum_i y_i}{r+n}
=\frac{r}{r+n}\frac{s}{r}
+\frac{n}{r+n}\bar y.
\] Here \(s/r\) is the prior mean and \(\bar y\) is the average observed count. With the prior fixed, more observation periods give the observed average more weight.

title: Appendix D — Deriving Conjugate Posteriors
section: D.4 A Normal likelihood and a Normal prior
text:
D.4 A Normal likelihood and a Normal prior
Suppose the observations are independent given their common mean \(\mu\), with a known sampling variance \(\sigma^2>0\): \[
Y_i\mid\mu\sim\text{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\] Assign \(\mu\) a \(\text{N}(\theta,\tau^2)\) prior, where \(\theta\) is the prior mean and \(\tau^2>0\) is the prior variance. Here \(\mu\) is the unknown parameter. The quantities \(\theta\), \(\tau^2\), and \(\sigma^2\) are specified by the model.
The likelihood and prior are \[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf y\mid\mu)
&=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
  \exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\mu)^2\right],\\
f(\mu)
&=(2\pi\tau^2)^{-1/2}
  \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mu-\theta)^2}{2\tau^2}\right].
\end{aligned}
\] The factors in front of the exponentials do not depend on \(\mu\). Taking logs turns multiplication of the kernels into addition: \[
\log f(\mu\mid\mathbf y)
=-\frac12\left[
\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}
+\frac{(\mu-\theta)^2}{\tau^2}
\right]+C.
\]

D.4.1 Collecting the terms in the unknown mean
To recognize a Normal density, we want one squared expression of the form \((\mu-m)^2\). First expand the squares already present: \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\mu)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2-2\mu\sum_{i=1}^n y_i+n\mu^2,\\
(\mu-\theta)^2&=\mu^2-2\theta\mu+\theta^2.
\end{aligned}
\] The first line contains \(n\mu^2\) because each of the \(n\) squared differences contributes one copy of \(\mu^2\). The terms \(\sum_i y_i^2\) and \(\theta^2\) do not depend on \(\mu\) and can be included in \(C\). Using \(\sum_i y_i=n\bar y\), the log posterior becomes \[
\log f(\mu\mid\mathbf y)
=-\frac12\left[
\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)\mu^2
-2\left(\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\theta}{\tau^2}\right)\mu
\right]+C.
\]


D.4.2 Completing the square
To make the next algebraic step easier to follow, name the two coefficients \[
A=\frac{n}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau^2},
\qquad
h=\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\theta}{\tau^2}.
\] The expression in brackets is \(A\mu^2-2h\mu\). Factor out \(A\) and add and subtract \((h/A)^2\) inside the brackets: \[
\begin{aligned}
A\mu^2-2h\mu
&=A\left[\mu^2-2\frac{h}{A}\mu\right]\\
&=A\left[\mu^2-2\frac{h}{A}\mu
          +\left(\frac{h}{A}\right)^2
          -\left(\frac{h}{A}\right)^2\right]\\
&=A\left(\mu-\frac{h}{A}\right)^2-\frac{h^2}{A}.
\end{aligned}
\] Adding and subtracting the same quantity leaves the expression unchanged, while the first three terms inside the brackets form a square. Since \(h^2/A\) does not depend on \(\mu\), it joins the constant in the log posterior. We are left with \[
\log f(\mu\mid\mathbf y)
=-\frac{A}{2}\left(\mu-\frac{h}{A}\right)^2+C.
\] A Normal log density with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\) has the form \(-(\mu-m)^2/(2v)+C\). Comparing the two expressions shows that \(m=h/A\) and \(v=1/A\). The parameter \(\mu\) can take any real value, as required for a Normal distribution. Thus \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu\mid\mathbf y&\sim\text{N}(m,v),\\
m&=\frac{\theta/\tau^2+n\bar y/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2+n/\sigma^2},
\qquad
v=\frac{1}{1/\tau^2+n/\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}
\] The normalized posterior density is therefore \[
f(\mu\mid\mathbf y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mu-m)^2}{2v}\right].
\]


D.4.3 Interpreting the update
The reciprocal of a variance is called precision. A small variance corresponds to high precision. The prior precision is \(1/\tau^2\). The sample mean has sampling variance \(\sigma^2/n\), so its precision is \(n/\sigma^2\). The posterior precision adds these contributions: \[
\frac1v=\frac1{\tau^2}+\frac n{\sigma^2}.
\] The posterior mean is a weighted average of \(\theta\) and \(\bar y\), with each weight proportional to its precision. A tightly concentrated prior gives \(\theta\) more weight. More observations, or less sampling variability, give \(\bar y\) more weight.
For the well-being example in Exercise 2.4, \(n=25\), \(\bar y=5.735\), and \(\sigma=0.5\). Taking the prior \(\mu\sim\text{N}(6.5,1^2)\) gives prior precision 1 and sample-mean precision \(25/0.5^2=100\). Hence \[
m=\frac{1\times6.5+100\times5.735}{101}
=\frac{580}{101}\approx5.743,
\qquad
v=\frac1{101}\approx0.00990.
\] The posterior mean lies close to the observed mean because the sample mean has much greater precision than the prior. The posterior standard deviation is \(\sqrt{v}\approx0.0995\); this is the value to pass to dnorm() as sd, whereas the Normal notation in the table uses the variance \(v\).
This derivation treats \(\sigma^2\) as known throughout. If the sampling variance is also unknown, it needs its own prior, and this one-parameter update no longer describes the full posterior.
